text:
Leo Frank, Jim Conley, and the missing minutes

You accept disputed times for Frank, then treat guesses about Conley as witnessed events. Conley was not a perfect witness. Both men face the same rules of evidence.

1906–1908: Start with the records

The 1906 Cornell University Senior Class Book, pages 344–345, entry 177, records Leo Max Frank at 5 feet 8 inches and 145 pounds. His passport application, sworn in Nuremberg on Friday, December 20, 1907, also gives his height as 5 feet 8 inches. The application bears a January 13, 1908 stamp. It gives no weight (Cornell, 1) (Frank, 2).

These records should be the starting point. The college weight dates from 1906, so it cannot be passed off as a confirmed weighing in April 1913. It should remain part of the discussion.

Using 107 pounds for Mary, as the defense did for its substitute body during a reenactment, gives a 38-pound difference from Frank’s college weight. Against the 4-foot-10-inch height in your post, his recorded height makes him ten inches taller. On the day of the murder, he was 29 and she was 13, approaching her fourteenth birthday (Cornell, 1) (Frank, 2) (BOE, 4, pp. 1, 145).

Height, weight, and reach can give an attacker an advantage. A grown man and a thirteen-year-old girl are also at different stages of physical growth. Neither person’s arm reach or strength was measured, so there is no honest way to assign either an exact strength score. There is even less reason to decide Frank was unable to hurt Mary by looking at his face (Hogrel, 5).

Saturday, April 26, 1913: Who was where?

The morning. Regular production had stopped for the holiday, but people were still inside. Day watchman E. F. Holloway placed himself there from 6:30 to 11:45 a.m. Harry Denham said he arrived around 7:30 a.m. to repair machinery with Arthur White. Hattie Hall performed office work for Frank later that morning (BOE, 4, pp. 29–31, 100–101, 108).

11:30–11:50 a.m. Mary’s mother placed her meal at 11:30 and her departure from home at 11:45. Mann said he left the factory at 11:30, leaving Frank and Hattie Hall. Mrs. White placed her first visit at 11:30–11:50. Corinthia Hall and Emma Clarke Freeman placed their visit at approximately 11:35–11:45 (BOE, 4, pp. 1, 21, 103–104, 122).

Mary’s trip downtown. George Epps said he left Mary at Forsyth and Marietta Streets around 12:07 p.m., when she walked toward the factory. Motorman Matthews instead placed her departure from the streetcar at Broad and Hunter around 12:10. Those accounts conflict. A later arrival at the factory is an argument, not an agreed fact (BOE, 4, pp. 1–2, 83–84).

12:02 p.m. Hattie Hall said she started leaving around noon, returned for her umbrella, and saw the clock showing two minutes past twelve when she left again (BOE, 4, p. 101).

12:05–12:10 p.m. Monteen Stover said she entered the outer and inner offices and found Frank absent. She checked the clock when she arrived and left. She was not simply standing in the hall, unable to see around an open safe door (BOE, 4, p. 26).

12:20–12:25 p.m., according to Quinn’s later estimate. Lemmie Quinn said he visited Frank’s office during this period. His timing, his delay in reporting it, and his earlier statements all need examination. His estimate cannot simply be treated as a clock reading (BOE, 4, pp. 107–108).

12:30–12:35 p.m. Mrs. White placed her return around 12:30. She saw Frank near the safe and then went upstairs. Frank later referred to a 12:35 version and allowed her memory might be better than his. Neither account places Conley in the basement (BOE, 4, p. 21) (Frank, 3, p. 186).

Around 12:50 p.m. to 1 p.m. Denham placed Frank’s visit upstairs around 12:50, while admitting uncertainty. Frank discussed leaving and locking the building. Mrs. White then left. These are separate sightings, not proof Frank was watched without a break throughout the noon hour (BOE, 4, pp. 21, 109).

Who saw someone downstairs?

At approximately 11:40 a.m., O. Tillander and E. K. Graham encountered a Black man on the ground floor who directed them upstairs. Both described someone about Conley’s size. Neither positively identified him as Conley. Graham said he noticed no drunkenness (BOE, 4, pp. 232–233).

When Mrs. White left near 1 p.m., she saw a man sitting on a box near the first-floor stairs. She later said he was about Conley’s size but could not identify him positively. Her account supports the presence of a man where Conley said he sat. It does not prove he remained there every minute (BOE, 4, pp. 21, 74).

Stover said she saw nobody. Quinn specifically said he did not see Conley. Their failure to notice him does not prove he was absent. Darley described darkness and large boxes around the elevator, enough to hide someone from a passing visitor (BOE, 4, pp. 26, 36, 107).

Your claim Conley was downstairs murdering Mary when Quinn and Mrs. White arrived is therefore a proposed explanation. No witness placed him there during those visits. Your further claim he missed Mrs. White because he was worked up after the murder is a guess about his thoughts.

Why the metal room was part of the prosecution’s account

Mary had stopped working because the metal had run out. Frank acknowledged she asked whether it had arrived. Her machine was in the metal department, and Grace Hicks said Frank walked through that department daily (BOE, 4, pp. 15–16) (Frank, 3, p. 185).

The prosecution’s theory was that Frank used this work question to get Mary into the metal room, or followed her there. This was tied to her job and the question she asked. It remains a theory because no independent witness saw him lead her there.

Part of Conley’s supposed 11:45 a.m.–1 p.m. opportunity also included Mary’s journey downtown. Unobserved time is not an opportunity to attack someone who has not reached the building.

Sunday, April 27: The drag trail pointed toward the elevator

Sergeant L. S. Dobbs described an apparent dragging trail beginning at the elevator and continuing toward the body. He explained:

“A man going down the ladder to the rear of the basement would not go in front of elevator where dragging was.”

Officer R. M. Lassiter also described dragging from the elevator. These observations existed apart from Conley’s later account (BOE, 4, pp. 8–9, 43).

This does not identify the person who moved Mary. It does mean the scuttle-hole theory must explain the trail’s starting point. An extra movement from the ladder toward the elevator would add another unwitnessed event to your story.

The opening itself measured two feet by two feet three inches, according to defense witness I. U. Kauffman. His testimony giving those dimensions does not establish the claimed fourteen-foot drop (BOE, 4, pp. 148–149).

The doctors reported an unfractured skull, but the cited findings do not show every bone was examined and found intact. Nor does every fall cause fractures. Hurt allowed a fall against a sharp floor or elevator edge could have caused the scalp wound (BOE, 4, pp. 46–49) (Williams, 6).

The stronger questions concern the drag trail, the lack of clear evidence at the scuttle hole, and the absence of anyone who actually saw the alleged push.

April 27–29: The notes, time card, and bloody shirt

The attempt to place suspicion on Newt Lee involved more than the notes.

On Sunday, April 27, Frank removed Lee’s time card and initially pronounced it correctly punched. Rogers said he also looked down the card and saw a punch for every number. Frank took it into his office. By Monday and Tuesday, Frank was describing gaps. Darley had also initially thought the record was correct, so an early mistaken reading remains another possible explanation (BOE, 4, pp. 13–14, 17, 33).

Black testified Frank said the missing time would have allowed Lee an hour to travel home and back. Black then gave conflicting answers about whether this discussion occurred ahead of or after the shirt search (BOE, 4, p. 19).

Black placed discovery of the bloody shirt at Lee’s home around 9 a.m. on Tuesday, April 29. Dr. Claude Smith described blood on the inside and found no armpit odor suggesting recent wear. These findings raised questions about how the shirt acquired its stains. They did not identify the person who put it in the barrel (BOE, 4, pp. 19, 45–46).

The Atlanta Journal of Thursday, July 31, 1913, in “Machinist Tells of Finding Blood, Hair and Pay Envelope On Second Floor, Where State Claims Girl Was Murdered,” recorded Dorsey’s position: “Our contention is that this shirt was a plant” (AJ, 7).

The prosecution argued the notes, the disputed time record, and the shirt helped direct suspicion toward Lee. I regard those circumstances as grounds for examining a frame-up. Nobody testified to watching Frank alter the card or plant the shirt, however. The accusation rests on the circumstances surrounding the three items.

Monday, April 28: The second-floor evidence was disputed, not imaginary

Barrett described new reddish spots near the girls’ dressing room, white material smeared over them, and several hairs on his lathe handle. Stanford and Mrs. Jefferson also described the spots. Barrett said the hair and spots were absent when he finished work on Friday (BOE, 4, pp. 26–29).

Smith found blood corpuscles but could not identify the blood as human or determine its age. Magnolia Kennedy said the hair looked like Mary’s but acknowledged she did not know whose it was. Barrett’s envelope fragment had no complete name, number, or amount (BOE, 4, pp. 27, 45–46, 104–105).

You are right about the lack of a conclusive identification. You go too far when you treat this limit as proof the objects had harmless origins. The defense offered other explanations. It did not establish the owner of every hair, spot, and envelope fragment.

Wednesday, April 30: What Lassiter said about the trash

The Atlanta Georgian published “Policeman Says Body Was Dragged From Elevator” on Wednesday, April 30, 1913. It placed Lassiter’s questioning at 3 p.m. He said he had been at the factory at 4:45 a.m. on Sunday, April 27. Asked what the bottom of the elevator shaft was made of, he answered:

“I don’t know. It was full of trash and I couldn’t see” (AG, 8).

At trial, Lassiter again described a large amount of trash at the bottom. He placed discovery of the uncrushed parasol between 6 and 7 a.m. Sunday. He was describing the pit beneath the elevator, not a tray inside the car (BOE, 4, p. 43).

The “shit in the shaft” argument runs this way: Conley said he used the basement that morning. Rogers saw apparently undisturbed excrement on Sunday, and the elevator later crushed it. Therefore, the argument goes, the elevator could not have carried Frank, Conley, and Mary into the basement on Saturday (BOE, 4, p. 15).

That argument has force. But the original scene was a rubbish-filled industrial pit, not a clean, measured surface. Lassiter gave no depth measurements for the trash. The cited testimony does not establish the clearance beneath every part of the car or show the pit remained unchanged between the two proposed descents.

Some rubbish could have stood higher than other rubbish. Searching the pit and moving objects could have changed it. Those are possible explanations worth testing. They do not prove the car stopped higher on Saturday, and loose rubbish might itself have been crushed.

I reject the claim that the stool proves every possible elevator trip impossible. I do not claim the trash proves Conley’s trip happened. The shaft evidence and the drag trail both need an explanation.

May 5–8: Why Quinn’s late alibi deserves doubt

The Atlanta Journal of Thursday, May 8, 1913, published “Lemmie Quinn Grilled by Coroner But He Sticks to His Statement.” Quinn said he had not told Lanford or the detectives about his Saturday visit until the previous Monday, May 5, nine days after the murder. He said he did not want to be pulled into the investigation (AJ, 9).

The Atlanta Georgian carried a more damaging claim the same day under “Black Testifies Quinn Denied Visiting Factory.” Black said Quinn had denied visiting the factory two or three times. Quinn denied making those statements (AG, 10) (BOE, 4, p. 107).

Quinn’s trial testimony also explains why his time should not be treated as exact. He admitted an earlier 12:00–12:25 range. He had forgotten a ten-to-fifteen-minute stop at Wolfsheimer’s, which his wife later brought to his attention. His arrival time was worked out from his route and errands, rather than read from a clock at Frank’s office (BOE, 4, pp. 107–108).

Then there is what Quinn said about helping Frank:

“As to whether I would have mentioned it or not, was up to Mr. Frank.”

State’s Exhibit S records Quinn saying Frank would consult his lawyers about whether mentioning the visit would be favorable. This was more complicated than an independent witness promptly reporting a clear clock reading (BOE, 4, pp. 107, 251).

Quinn had answers. He feared long questioning and possible detention. He denied Frank ordered him to keep quiet. Freeman said Quinn told her he had just seen Frank. Conley also claimed to see Quinn, although he placed Quinn’s visit earlier than Mary’s. Those points support considering a visit. They do not settle its minute (AJ, 9) (BOE, 4, pp. 54, 104, 107–108).

I do not accept Quinn’s late estimate as a firm stopping point for Frank’s opportunity. The delay, the alleged denials, the forgotten stop, and the discussion with Frank give reasons to question whether the time was adjusted afterward. They do not prove the whole visit was invented.

Eighteen minutes, twenty-three minutes, or roughly half an hour?

Leonard Dinnerstein gave “about eighteen minutes”, approximately 12:02–12:20, in the revised edition of The Leo Frank Case, page 49. Even this account favorable to Frank gives a longer gap than your five-to-ten-minute claim (Dinnerstein, 11).

The arithmetic depends on which sightings are accepted. 12:02–12:20 is eighteen minutes. 12:02–12:25 is twenty-three. Without Quinn’s disputed time, Mrs. White’s next sighting at 12:30–12:35 leaves twenty-eight to thirty-three minutes after Hall’s departure. Counting from noon gives thirty to thirty-five minutes, but Hall’s presence until about 12:02 must be included (BOE, 4, pp. 21, 101, 107–108).

These are gaps in observation, not proof of what Frank did. Mary’s arrival also limits the time available for an attack. But your claim of only five to ten minutes depends on accepting disputed times as settled facts.

May 6–9: Mann gave investigators an account in 1913

The Pinkerton reports record interviews with Mann on May 6, May 7, and May 9, 1913. They do more than repeat his factory departure time.

The May 7 account says he left at 11:30, met his mother at the Vaudette Theatre at noon, and went with her to his brother’s workplace at Thompson’s Printing Company. It then places him on other errands, including the gas office around 12:35. The May 9 account again says he met his mother at noon (Pinkerton, 12).

These reports name people and places investigators could have checked soon after the murder. They also conflict with the explanation Mann gave in 1982 for returning to the factory.

May–August 1913: The complaints about Frank’s conduct

Your claim Frank preferred heavy-set adult women does not establish he would never approach a younger employee. It also leaves out allegations made against him during the original investigation.

At the inquest, Nellie Wood accused Frank of unwanted touching in his office during her brief employment. Mamie Kitchens later testified he opened the dressing-room door while Irene Jackson was undressed, stood there, and laughed. On cross-examination, Kitchens also said he asked whether they had work to do. These were specific complaints, although they were disputed and did not prove Mary’s murder (Wood, 13) (BOE, 4, p. 222).

C. B. Dalton described women and drinks in Frank’s office and his own visits to the basement with Daisy Hopkins. Conley described acting as a lookout during visits involving women. Their evidence does not establish every woman mentioned was a prostitute. Dalton’s record and truthfulness were challenged, and numerous employees spoke favorably about Frank (BOE, 4, pp. 50–53, 220–221).

Conley was not a man without a record. State’s Exhibit T listed several disorderly-conduct cases. Nor would the absence of a known sexual complaint against him prove he could not commit an assault. My point is that the complaints about Frank cannot be erased by describing him as harmless-looking or assigning him an exclusive preference for adult women (BOE, 4, p. 251).

August 1913: I do not need Conley to be a perfect witness

Conley’s changing stories, the late additions, and the conflicting times are real problems. His claim about hiding in a wardrobe during a visit by Corinthia Hall and Emma Freeman conflicts with their morning departure. His 12:56 clock claim also creates trouble when compared with Frank’s claimed 1:20 arrival home (BOE, 4, pp. 55–57, 103–104, 109).

The extra cord in Frank’s hand is an odd detail. It could be an added detail which was not true. I cannot settle it by assuming Conley told the truth about everything. But challenging this detail does not establish your separate story of a witnessed push through the scuttle hole.

Conley placed the scream earlier than Stover’s visit and the tiptoeing after she left. Your version moves the tiptoeing into her visit and treats her failure to hear the earlier scream as a contradiction. It is not a contradiction within the order he gave, although the scream itself remains his disputed claim (BOE, 4, pp. 54, 71).

The fourth-floor men were hammering. Denham admitted considerable noise could have occurred below without their noticing. His failure to hear the elevator deserves consideration, but he was not watching and listening to the car without interruption (BOE, 4, pp. 108–109).

The defense’s reenactment took 18½ minutes, excluding the claimed wardrobe interval and actual note-writing. Adding its estimates for those tasks produced 36½ minutes. This challenged Conley’s timetable. It did not show the route itself could not be followed (BOE, 4, pp. 143–146).

The notes and cigarette box

Conley said Frank wanted him to return and burn the body. He also said Frank proposed placing the notes with it if Conley failed to return. That gives two possible plans. Distance from the furnace does not disprove a burning proposal which was never carried out (BOE, 4, pp. 57–58).

Conley said he did not know what finally happened to the notes. Frank placing them was part of the prosecution’s explanation, not something Conley claimed to watch (BOE, 4, p. 58).

Conley also said he found two dollar bills and two quarters, $2.50, in a cigarette box Frank gave him. Your claim he bought drinks with Mary’s $1.20 is another theory, not a payment traced by a witness (BOE, 4, pp. 57–58).

Monday, August 18: The toilet explanation was not an alibi

Frank’s earlier police statement placed Mary’s arrival between 12:05 and 12:10, perhaps 12:07. This overlaps Stover’s empty-office visit. Scott also said Frank initially insisted he had remained in the office throughout noon to 12:30 (Frank, 3, p. 243) (BOE, 4, p. 24).

In his August 18 statement, Frank allowed he might have gone to the toilet without remembering it. He did not recall a specific toilet visit covering Stover’s five minutes (Frank, 3, p. 186).

Hicks placed the men’s and women’s toilets in the same rear area, with a partition between them. The route toward the office passed the dressing room and Mary’s machine within two or three feet. A possible toilet visit therefore allowed Frank to be near the area where the prosecution placed the attack. It did not establish he was somewhere else (BOE, 4, pp. 15–16).

June–August 1915: The elevator objection and the bite allegation

In his June 21, 1915 commutation statement, Governor John M. Slaton accepted the unmashed-excrement objection as serious evidence against Conley’s elevator account. He described riding the elevator with Dorsey and William M. Howard, then again with his secretary. Those tests could show how the machinery worked. They could not restore the exact rubbish-filled pit as it stood more than two years earlier (Slaton, 14).

The claim about a bite on a girl’s inner thigh has a different source. It appears in Tom Watson’s August 1915 account, which says a girl from the Cincinnati home described it while the jury was outside. It is absent from Hewell’s recorded testimony to the jury. This was Watson’s later allegation, not a proved injury or a medical finding (Watson, 15) (BOE, 4, pp. 222–223).

1965: Golden made Frank shorter

Harry Golden’s A Little Girl Is Dead, page 7, describes Frank as five feet six inches tall and thin. Published in 1965, it appeared 59 years after the Cornell record and 52 years after the murder. Its height differs by two inches from both early records (Golden, 16) (Cornell, 1) (Frank, 2).

The difference is there on the page. No guess about Golden’s intentions is needed to point it out.

1982: Mann’s later story conflicts with his earlier one

Mann’s March 4, 1982 affidavit said he failed to meet his mother and returned to the factory. He described seeing Conley holding a limp girl near the trapdoor, receiving a threat, and fleeing home. Compare this with the 1913 reports placing him with his mother at the theater and then at his brother’s workplace (Mann, 17) (Pinkerton, 12).

This is more than leaving out an unpleasant event. One account says he met his mother. The other uses his failure to meet her as the reason he returned to the factory. Both cannot be accurate accounts of the same trip.

His earlier story named people and stops which could have been checked soon after the murder. The later factory scene rests on his account nearly sixty-nine years afterward. I do not accept it as established simply because he signed an affidavit.

Most important, Mann never claimed to see Conley push Mary through the opening, strike her, strangle her, write the notes, or take her money. He described holding a body and what he thought Conley intended to do. Even accepting his account would not identify who first attacked Mary or exclude help from another person (Mann, 17).

The parents’ conduct also deserves questioning. Why allow their son to return to work near a man he said had threatened to kill him? Sunday was not his next working day. His later questioning addressed his return on a following workday (Mann, 17).

Mann’s explanation was that his parents wanted to keep their son out of the investigation. I question how that fits with letting him return to the same workplace. But the family’s race does not prove how they would respond to fear. The conflict between his two accounts is a stronger argument than assuming a White family in Jim Crow Atlanta could never remain silent.

2003–2026: A smaller Frank and a judgment from his face

Steve Oney’s And the Dead Shall Rise, page 10, gives five feet six inches and 120 pounds. Published in 2003, it appeared 97 years after the Cornell entry. It presents a man two inches shorter and twenty-five pounds lighter than the college record (Oney, 18) (Cornell, 1).

The lower 125–130-pound estimate has an earlier source: Darley’s 1913 testimony. It was given during cross-examination and helped Frank’s defense. It was still an estimate, not a recorded weighing. I question treating it as exact, but it cannot honestly be called a modern invention (BOE, 4, p. 36).

Even using that lower estimate against 107 pounds, Frank was 18–23 pounds heavier. Using Hicks’s estimate of 115 pounds for Mary reduces the difference to 10–15 pounds. His recorded height still exceeds the height in your post by ten inches. He was a grown man of twenty-nine, and she was thirteen. None of these comparisons establishes he was unable to hurt her (Cornell, 1) (Frank, 2) (BOE, 4, pp. 1, 16, 36).

Pincher Martin’s claim that “a walk around the block would wear him out” asks an old photograph to serve as a fitness test. Calling Frank “nebbish” or “weaselly” measures nothing. The college-history account reports tennis and class basketball, although it does not reproduce the underlying basketball record. That reported sports history is another reason to question the frail picture, not a personal strength test either (Archive, 19).

This is what I object to in the “Leo Frank girlyman hoax” argument: lower his size in the reader’s mind, then treat the resulting picture as proof he could not hurt Mary. The records, the dates, and the source of each estimate should remain visible.

text:
@PMOIndia Respected Sir,
Subject: Urgent appeal to protect the lives, homes and lifelong savings of nearly 3,000 residents of PWS, 7 Hills Apartments, from the proposed 100-foot road widening—Kokapet, Narsingi
I write with deep pain and anxiety as a retired professor and a resident of Power Welfare Society (PWS), 7 Hills Apartments, Kokapet, Narsingi, Hyderabad. The proposed 100-foot road adjoining our society has left us frightened about the safety of our buildings, the future of our homes and the security of nearly 3,000 residents. I respectfully seek your immediate intervention before any action causes damage that cannot be undone.
PWS was registered in 2005 under the Andhra Pradesh Societies Act by employees of the Central Power Sector. Its housing project was launched on 1 June 2009 and comprises seven high-rise towers with 853 apartments. Many families invested their lifelong earnings and retirement savings here, trusting the validity of the land documents and the approvals under which the project was built. For about 15 years, the society has been paying municipal taxes, water charges and other applicable charges. We believed that a lawfully established home would offer us peace and security in our later years.
Large residential projects have since come up, or are being developed, around our society. We understand that a notification has been issued requiring PWS and neighbouring landowners to surrender land for a proposed 100-foot road. Municipal personnel have begun marking the affected areas. The proposed alignment appears to affect our society from both the front (RR Corp)  and the rear (Alekya Homes). Residents are deeply concerned that an established community is being made to bear a severe burden to meet the access needs of surrounding developments.
According to our present understanding of the markings and proposed alignment, the affected area includes land close to or beneath parts of our buildings and basement parking. Residents fear that more than 100 parking spaces could be lost when the impact on both sides is considered. Our Lord Ganesha temple, electrical installation serving the apartments, part of the children’s park and many mature trees also appear to be at risk. The extent of the impact must be established through an official joint survey and clearly explained to every affected resident.
Our gravest concern is the safety of the towers, particularly F, E and A/B blocks. Any cutting into or excavation near a shared basement or building foundation raises serious questions about structural stability. Residents also need clear answers about fire-engine access, emergency evacuation, electricity supply and safe movement within the society. These concerns require an independent assessment by qualified structural and fire-safety experts before any demolition, excavation or removal takes place. For us, this is a potential threat to human life.
I live in Flat 102, F Block, having invested my hard-earned post-retirement savings in this home. At this stage of life, the fear of losing the safety of my home is deeply distressing. A home holds a family’s memories, a lifetime of sacrifice and the hope of spending one’s remaining years with dignity. It is painful to feel that everything we worked for could be placed at risk by a decision over which we have little control.
Many of our neighbours are retired power-sector employees who spent their working lives serving the country. There are elderly residents, children and families who depend on this community for security and support. The continued marking exercise has created fear and uncertainty. We worry about what may happen next and whether our concerns will be heard before machinery arrives. No family should have to live with such anxiety inside its own home.
A wide road running close to our buildings on both sides would also expose residents to traffic, noise, dust and loss of privacy. Children’s play areas and the green spaces that make the society liveable could be reduced. The loss of basement parking could create further congestion and obstruct movement within the premises. These consequences deserve a careful assessment alongside the proposed road’s benefits.
We recognise the need for better roads and planned development. But development must protect the people who already live in an area. It would be deeply unjust if the needs of new projects were met by placing established homes and residents’ safety at risk. We request a transparent explanation of why this alignment was chosen, what alternatives were examined and how the burden on existing communities was considered. Our concern about possible undue influence should be examined impartially, on the basis of records and evidence.
We understand that neighbouring landowners, including Tera Nagarjuna Reddy and others, have approached the Hon’ble High Court of Telangana in Writ Petition No. 32694 of 2026, CNR No. HBHC010671982026. We have been informed that directions concerning due process and maintenance of status quo have been issued. I request the authorities to examine the actual order, clarify its scope and comply strictly with every applicable direction. The continuing marking activity has increased residents’ anxiety, and we seek a written explanation of its purpose and the action proposed.
I respectfully request that you direct an immediate pause on any demolition, excavation, taking possession or alteration affecting PWS until the residents’ objections, the relevant court directions and the safety implications have been examined. Please arrange a joint site inspection with society representatives and independent experts. We also request copies of the notification, the approved road alignment, the survey showing the exact land affected and the technical reports relied upon. Residents should be given a meaningful opportunity to present their concerns and receive a reasoned written response.
Above all, please examine an alternative alignment that protects our occupied buildings, shared basements, essential facilities and community spaces. Our homes must not be treated as expendable simply because they stand in the path of a proposed road. The responsibility of the authorities is to find a solution that serves the public without placing an existing community in danger.
No compensation can remove our agony. No amount of money can restore the peace of an elderly person who fears that the home built with a lifetime’s savings may become unsafe. Nor can it replace the security, memories and bonds that hold this community together. Our appeal is for the preservation of our homes and the protection of our lives.
Our society has limited funds to sustain a prolonged legal battle. That should not make our voices less worthy of being heard. We seek fair treatment, transparent decisions and protection of our lives and homes. We are determined to pursue every peaceful and lawful means available to us. We will fight till the end to protect our homes, our dignity and the safety of our families.
Sir, please treat this as an urgent appeal from a resident whose peace of mind and retirement security are at stake. Behind every affected flat is a family. Behind every retirement investment are decades of work and sacrifice. I request your personal intervention, a written assurance that residents’ safety will be protected and an early meeting with our society representatives.
Please do not allow our remaining years to be consumed by fear and a struggle to save the homes we worked all our lives to secure. Act before an avoidable loss becomes an irreversible tragedy. We place our hope in your sense of justice and your duty to protect the people.
Yours faithfully,

Subject: Urgent appeal to protect the lives, homes and lifelong savings of nearly 3,000 residents of PWS, 7 Hills Apartments, from the proposed 100-foot road widening—Kokapet, Narsingi
I write with deep pain and anxiety as a retired professor and a resident of Power Welfare Society (PWS), 7 Hills Apartments, Kokapet, Narsingi, Hyderabad. The proposed 100-foot road adjoining our society has left us frightened about the safety of our buildings, the future of our homes and the security of nearly 3,000 residents. I respectfully seek your immediate intervention before any action causes damage that cannot be undone.
PWS was registered in 2005 under the Andhra Pradesh Societies Act by employees of the Central Power Sector. Its housing project was launched on 1 June 2009 and comprises seven high-rise towers with 853 apartments. Many families invested their lifelong earnings and retirement savings here, trusting the validity of the land documents and the approvals under which the project was built. For about 15 years, the society has been paying municipal taxes, water charges and other applicable charges. We believed that a lawfully established home would offer us peace and security in our later years.
Large residential projects have since come up, or are being developed, around our society. We understand that a notification has been issued requiring PWS and neighbouring landowners to surrender land for a proposed 100-foot road. Municipal personnel have begun marking the affected areas. The proposed alignment appears to affect our society from both the front (RR Corp)  and the rear (Alekya Homes). Residents are deeply concerned that an established community is being made to bear a severe burden to meet the access needs of surrounding developments.
According to our present understanding of the markings and proposed alignment, the affected area includes land close to or beneath parts of our buildings and basement parking. Residents fear that more than 100 parking spaces could be lost when the impact on both sides is considered. Our Lord Ganesha temple, electrical installation serving the apartments, part of the children’s park and many mature trees also appear to be at risk. The extent of the impact must be established through an official joint survey and clearly explained to every affected resident.
Our gravest concern is the safety of the towers, particularly F, E and A/B blocks. Any cutting into or excavation near a shared basement or building foundation raises serious questions about structural stability. Residents also need clear answers about fire-engine access, emergency evacuation, electricity supply and safe movement within the society. These concerns require an independent assessment by qualified structural and fire-safety experts before any demolition, excavation or removal takes place. For us, this is a potential threat to human life.
I live in Flat 102, F Block, having invested my hard-earned post-retirement savings in this home. At this stage of life, the fear of losing the safety of my home is deeply distressing. A home holds a family’s memories, a lifetime of sacrifice and the hope of spending one’s remaining years with dignity. It is painful to feel that everything we worked for could be placed at risk by a decision over which we have little control.
Many of our neighbours are retired power-sector employees who spent their working lives serving the country. There are elderly residents, children and families who depend on this community for security and support. The continued marking exercise has created fear and uncertainty. We worry about what may happen next and whether our concerns will be heard before machinery arrives. No family should have to live with such anxiety inside its own home.
A wide road running close to our buildings on both sides would also expose residents to traffic, noise, dust and loss of privacy. Children’s play areas and the green spaces that make the society liveable could be reduced. The loss of basement parking could create further congestion and obstruct movement within the premises. These consequences deserve a careful assessment alongside the proposed road’s benefits.
We recognise the need for better roads and planned development. But development must protect the people who already live in an area. It would be deeply unjust if the needs of new projects were met by placing established homes and residents’ safety at risk. We request a transparent explanation of why this alignment was chosen, what alternatives were examined and how the burden on existing communities was considered. Our concern about possible undue influence should be examined impartially, on the basis of records and evidence.
We understand that neighbouring landowners, including Tera Nagarjuna Reddy and others, have approached the Hon’ble High Court of Telangana in Writ Petition No. 32694 of 2026, CNR No. HBHC010671982026. We have been informed that directions concerning due process and maintenance of status quo have been issued. I request the authorities to examine the actual order, clarify its scope and comply strictly with every applicable direction. The continuing marking activity has increased residents’ anxiety, and we seek a written explanation of its purpose and the action proposed.
I respectfully request that you direct an immediate pause on any demolition, excavation, taking possession or alteration affecting PWS until the residents’ objections, the relevant court directions and the safety implications have been examined. Please arrange a joint site inspection with society representatives and independent experts. We also request copies of the notification, the approved road alignment, the survey showing the exact land affected and the technical reports relied upon. Residents should be given a meaningful opportunity to present their concerns and receive a reasoned written response.
Above all, please examine an alternative alignment that protects our occupied buildings, shared basements, essential facilities and community spaces. Our homes must not be treated as expendable simply because they stand in the path of a proposed road. The responsibility of the authorities is to find a solution that serves the public without placing an existing community in danger.
No compensation can remove our agony. No amount of money can restore the peace of an elderly person who fears that the home built with a lifetime’s savings may become unsafe. Nor can it replace the security, memories and bonds that hold this community together. Our appeal is for the preservation of our homes and the protection of our lives.
Our society has limited funds to sustain a prolonged legal battle. That should not make our voices less worthy of being heard. We seek fair treatment, transparent decisions and protection of our lives and homes. We are determined to pursue every peaceful and lawful means available to us. We will fight till the end to protect our homes, our dignity and the safety of our families.
Sir, please treat this as an urgent appeal from a resident whose peace of mind and retirement security are at stake. Behind every affected flat is a family. Behind every retirement investment are decades of work and sacrifice. I request your personal intervention, a written assurance that residents’ safety will be protected and an early meeting with our society representatives.
Please do not allow our remaining years to be consumed by fear and a struggle to save the homes we worked all our lives to secure. Act before an avoidable loss becomes an irreversible tragedy. We place our hope in your sense of justice and your duty to protect the people.
Yours faithfully,
Dr. V. S. P. Rao
Flat 102, F Block
Power Welfare Society, 7 Hills Apartments
Kokapet, Narsingi, Hyderabad

I write with deep pain and anxiety as a retired professor and a resident of Power Welfare Society (PWS), 7 Hills Apartments, Kokapet, Narsingi, Hyderabad. The proposed 100-foot road adjoining our society has left us frightened about the safety of our buildings, the future of our homes and the security of nearly 3,000 residents. I respectfully seek your immediate intervention before any action causes damage that cannot be undone.
PWS was registered in 2005 under the Andhra Pradesh Societies Act by employees of the Central Power Sector. Its housing project was launched on 1 June 2009 and comprises seven high-rise towers with 853 apartments. Many families invested their lifelong earnings and retirement savings here, trusting the validity of the land documents and the approvals under which the project was built. For about 15 years, the society has been paying municipal taxes, water charges and other applicable charges. We believed that a lawfully established home would offer us peace and security in our later years.
Large residential projects have since come up, or are being developed, around our society. We understand that a notification has been issued requiring PWS and neighbouring landowners to surrender land for a proposed 100-foot road. Municipal personnel have begun marking the affected areas. The proposed alignment appears to affect our society from both the front (RR Corp)  and the rear (Alekya Homes). Residents are deeply concerned that an established community is being made to bear a severe burden to meet the access needs of surrounding developments.
According to our present understanding of the markings and proposed alignment, the affected area includes land close to or beneath parts of our buildings and basement parking. Residents fear that more than 100 parking spaces could be lost when the impact on both sides is considered. Our Lord Ganesha temple, electrical installation serving the apartments, part of the children’s park and many mature trees also appear to be at risk. text:
SMART ENGINEERING 🧠 Tesla has figured out a "quantized" way to run AI attention on low-power 8-bit chips while holding on to near 16-bit accuracy: a fresh ruler for every token, tile by tile ⚡

Attention is how a transformer, the AI architecture behind modern chatbots, decides which parts of an input matter most, and Tesla’s version is tailored specifically for vehicles and robots. It splits input data into tokens (small chunks of data) and compares each token against every other one. That comparison table expands fast: double the input length, and the table quadruples in size.

Flash attention, a popular optimization technique, avoids storing this entire table by processing it tile by tile and keeping running totals along the way.

The catch is that flash attention was originally built for hardware running precise 16-bit floating-point math, which is a poor fit for low-power edge devices. Energy-efficient chips rely instead on fast 8-bit integer operations. However, 8 bits offer only 256 discrete levels, much like a ruler with just 256 tick marks. Every value gets rounded to the nearest tick, which is why earlier 8-bit flash attention designs struggled to maintain accuracy.

Tesla’s quantized flash attention patent (US 2026/0299946 A1) comes from the same four inventors behind two related quantization patents mentioned in a previous post, and it applies their per-token ruler approach directly inside each tile.

Before comparing tokens, each token's comparison values (its query and key vectors) get a custom-scaled ruler calibrated so the most extreme value aligns with the final tick mark. The comparison then runs using fast 8-bit math, and the resulting scores are output in a higher-precision format.

Next, an operation known as softmax converts those scores into weights (the proportion of attention assigned to each token) using exponential functions. Exponentials scale up rapidly, so flash attention tracks a running maximum (the highest score seen so far) and normalizes everything against it to prevent numbers from overflowing.

Tesla’s implementation keeps this running maximum in 16-bit precision, since the patent notes that reducing it further degrades overall quality. Finally, these weights receive the same per-token ruler treatment and are multiplied in 8-bit math against each token’s content (its value vector) to produce the final output.

Tile size matters just as much, because it dictates how many values share a single ruler. Small tiles require constant recalibration, where every pass introduces minor rounding errors. Conversely, oversized tiles pack too many values onto a single ruler, making it difficult to capture subtle details and outliers.

The patent evaluates accuracy using the signal-to-noise ratio relative to standard 16-bit attention, where a higher score reflects a closer match. That fidelity climbs from about 13 dB with 32 tokens per tile to a peak of roughly 31 dB at 256, before slipping to around 29 dB at 2,048 tokens.

The payoff, according to the patent, is attention that runs on low-power integer chips and handles longer inputs without taking a performance hit, even on compact onboard computers with limited fast memory. For a car or a robot, that means taking in more of the world at once without waiting for a bigger chip.

It's smart engineering rather than a single massive breakthrough. Across three patents, the same humble ruler, resized for every token, now reaches from the basic number format all the way into the heart of the transformer. That is how low-cost 8-bit hardware ends up tackling work that once required high-precision chips.

text:
GOOD NEWS 🧮 Tesla has figured out how to shrink AI's numbers without losing detail: give every token its own ruler and trim a bit the AI rarely uses 🔥

The neural networks powering Tesla's cars and robots keep growing, and the ongoing challenge is fitting them onto onboard computers without needing a hardware upgrade every cycle.

Two patent applications from the same four inventors tackle this challenge from complementary angles: a mixed-precision transformer (US 2026/0299881 A1) and a compact number format (US 2026/0299533 A1).

A common way to accelerate neural networks is to run their heavy math using 8-bit integers, which chips can crunch rapidly. But 8 bits offer only 256 distinct values, like a ruler with just 256 tick marks, forcing every number to round to the nearest tick.

The traditional static approach sets the ruler’s length in advance. That falls short when inputs shift: a scale calibrated for bright daylight compresses a dark night scene into just a handful of ticks, wiping out critical details.

The mixed-precision transformer solves this by resizing the ruler on the fly. Input data arrives as tokens (compact chunks of data). For each token, the system identifies its most extreme value and scales the ruler so that value lands on the very last tick mark. Every token gets its own tailored ruler, and no tick marks go to waste.

Crucially, only the heavy matrix multiplications, where the bulk of the compute happens, drop down to 8 bits. Sensitive operations like normalization, softmax, and the running totals carried between layers stay in higher precision, preserving the numerical stability the network needs.

Many of those higher-precision operations rely on a format called BF15, introduced in the number-format patent. Computers store floating-point numbers much like scientific notation: an exponent defines the overall magnitude, while the remaining bits capture precision.

The standard 16-bit format, BF16, allocates 8 bits to the exponent, providing a dynamic range spanning roughly 10⁻³⁸ to 10³⁸. But running inference on a trained model rarely demands that broad of a reach.

Trimming a single exponent bit leaves a 15-bit format dubbed E7M7. It still covers a range of roughly 10⁻¹⁹ to 10¹⁹, but makes every value lighter to store and move across memory channels. Because it preserves all 7 of BF16’s precision bits, trained BF16 models can run in E7M7 without any training-inference mismatch.

The number-format patent also outlines how to make E7M7 computationally cheap to handle in hardware. A value converts into a standard 32-bit float with a single shift, followed by two additions to restore its sign and translate the exponent back into standard form.

From there, converting values into integers reuses the transformer’s ruler trick: scale everything so the peak value lands on the final tick. Because every number gets multiplied by that scale factor anyway, an optimized hardware implementation folds the exponent fix directly into the scale itself, letting each value skip an addition entirely.

Together, the two innovations divide and conquer. 

One packs each token into 8-bit integers for heavy math without wasting dynamic range, while the other makes surrounding high-precision calculations smaller and faster to process. Both cut memory traffic, reduce power consumption, and speed up predictions, letting Tesla scale up its models while keeping existing chips in place.

text:
To Elon Musk

Hello, Mr. Musk.

I am a Tesla owner, fan, and shareholder in Korea.

Korea is Tesla’s third-largest market after the United States and China. 

Koreans understand technology quickly and adopt new products early. 
Just as Korea was a testbed in the mobile era, the same pattern is showing up with Tesla.

Demand for Full Self-Driving (Supervised) here is intense. 
Model S and Model X sold strongly right up to discontinuation, and used prices have at times exceeded new-car prices. 

Owners are not asking for a slogan. 
They are asking to use a feature they already paid for, or are ready to pay for.

Tesla’s own data should show that demand, and the willingness to buy FSD, clearly.

The obstacle is not consumer interest. 
It is the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport.

Tesla Korea has not been passive.

According to Korean reports this week, the company proposed cooperation at least twice: in November 2025, it offered a domestic safety review and test vehicles; in July 2026, before FSD V14 Lite, it again offered technical and safety materials and renewed the offer of vehicles for a government review.

Those offers were not taken up. 
The ministry’s position has been that it is not in separate consultations with Tesla Korea. 

The Korea Transportation Safety Authority has no record of directly testing, evaluating, or analyzing FSD. 
Verification on the government side remains at zero, even after Tesla offered the cars.

That is not caution. 
It is indifference and non-response. 

Taiwan is already in technical review and on-road validation with Tesla. 
Korea, a much larger Tesla market, will not even start a test.

Because of that stance, a near-term path for FSD on the cars Koreans actually buy looks blocked.

Vehicles supplied to Korea today come from Giga Shanghai. 

They are configured to European rules, without the FSD hardware and software package Korean buyers want. 
Many people here would pay more for a car that can actually run FSD.

So this is the request:

Please export U.S.-built Teslas, from Fremont or Texas, to Korea, with the FSD configuration owners are asking for.

If U.S. demand is softer this year, diverting some of that volume to Korea is a rational use of capacity. 

Demand is strong in Europe, Korea, Japan, and ASEAN, and Shanghai alone cannot cover all of it. 
Even with logistics and regional supply chains, U.S.-built cars equipped for FSD would matter here.

This is not only an export request. 

If the Korean government keeps refusing even to test, shipping cars that respect the choice customers have already made is another card Tesla can play.

Korean owners genuinely want this technology.
Meeting that demand would deepen a loyal base in Tesla’s third-largest market.

I trust your judgment and Tesla’s ability to move fast. 

I hope the day comes soon when we can drive FSD-equipped Teslas on Korean roads.

Thank you for your time. 

I am always rooting for you.

Sincerely,

A Tesla fan and shareholder in Korea

text:
「1日2リットル、水を飲もう」。その元ネタとされる1945年の文書には、実は続きがありました。
「この量の大部分は、調理された食べ物に含まれている」💧
今日は「水はどれだけ飲めばいいのか」を、研究から見ていきます。後半では、こまめに飲むための水筒をひとつ紹介します。

■ 「コップ8杯」はどこから来た?
英語圏には「8×8」という言い方があります。約240mLのコップで1日8杯、合計約1.9リットルです。
2002年、米国の生理学者バルティンが、この話の根拠を探しました。古い文献まで調べ、専門家にも問い合わせています。
結論は「『少なくとも8杯』を支持する科学的な研究は、見つからなかった」でした。
ここで想定しているのは、温暖な気候で、主に座って過ごす健康な大人です。

その中で、起源の候補として紹介されたのが1945年の文書です。米国の食品栄養委員会は、こう書きました。
「大人に適した水の量は、多くの場合1日2.5リットル」。
そして最後に「この量の大部分は、調理された食べ物に含まれている」。
この最後の一文が見落とされ、「水を飲む量」の話に変わったのでは、という説があります。
ただし、これは一つの仮説です。確定した歴史ではありません。
バルティン自身も、暑い場所や激しい運動、一部の病気では、もっと多く必要になりうると書いています。

■ 5,604人の「水の出入り」を測った研究
では実際に、人の体ではどれくらいの水が出入りしているのでしょう。
2022年、科学誌サイエンスに大きな研究が載りました(ヤマダら)。日本の研究者が筆頭著者を務めた国際チームです。
集めたのは、23か国、生後8日から96歳までの5,604人のデータです。

測り方が面白いんです。目印のついた水を、少しだけ飲んでもらいます。
目印は「重水素」という、ふつうより少し重い水素です。
その目印が尿などから抜けていく速さを追うと、体の水が1日にどれだけ入れ替わったかが分かります。
これを「水の入れ替わり量」と呼びます。

ここで大事な注意があります。入れ替わり量は「飲んだ量」ではありません。
食べ物に含まれる水や、体の中で栄養を使うときにできる水も、全部ふくみます。

結果は「人によって、かなり違う」でした。
論文の例では、20歳・体重70kgで、ふだんの活動量の男性なら、1日約3.2リットル。
同じ条件で体重60kgの女性なら、約2.7リットルです。
(平均気温10℃、暮らしの水準が高い国に住む、運動選手ではない人、という前提の予測です)
同じ20歳でも、運動選手が、暑くて湿気の多い標高2,000mの土地で暮らすと、予測は約7リットルまで増えます。
体の大きさ、活動量、気温や湿度、年齢で、数字は大きく動くのです。

ただし、これは多くの人のデータを比べて、傾向を見るタイプの研究です。
式で説明できたのは、人による違いの半分弱でした。
また、食べ物と飲み物の内訳は分けて測れていない、と論文に書かれています。
なので、この数字をそのまま「飲むべき量」にはできません。

■ 日本の食事なら、どうなる?
厚生労働省の資料に、1日の水の出入りの例があります。合計約2.5リットルの内訳は、
・飲み水から 約1.2リットル
・食事から 約1.0リットル
・体の中でできる水 約0.3リットル
です。
飲み物の分は、500mLのペットボトルで2本半ほど。ご飯やみそ汁、野菜にも、水はたっぷり入っています。
「2リットル全部を水で飲む」のとは、だいぶ印象が違いますよね。
(これは目安の一例で、人によって変わります)

■ 「たくさん飲めば健康に」は確かめられた?
2024年、米国のハカムらが、水を飲む量を変えた試験を集めて調べました(JAMAネットワーク・オープン誌)。
対象は、くじ引きで人を2つの組に分ける試験(ランダム化比較試験)18件です。
1件あたりの人数は、真ん中の値で48人。小さめの試験が多い分野です。
試験ごとに対象も目的もばらばらだったので、数字を一つにまとめる計算はしていません。

結果がそろって見えたのは、限られた場面でした。
・過体重の大人が、低カロリーの食事と合わせて、食事の前に水を飲んだ減量の試験
・一度、腎臓結石ができた人の再発
ほかに、ふだん水をあまり飲まず、膀胱炎をくり返す女性で、再発が減った試験が1件ありました。
一方、頭痛については、結果がそろっていません。

まとめると、「誰でも多めに飲めば、体に良いことが起きる」とまでは、まだ確かめられていません。
効くかどうかは「誰が、何のために」で変わる、というのが今の段階です。

■ のどの渇きは、意外と先回りする
水を飲むと、すぐにのどの渇きがおさまりますよね。
でも、飲んだ水が腸から吸収されて、血液が薄まるまでには時間がかかります。
では、なぜすぐに楽になるのでしょう。

2016年のネイチャー誌に、マウスの実験があります(ジマーマンら)。
のどの渇きを生む脳の神経細胞は、水をなめた最初の瞬間から静まり始めました。
そして1分以内に、はっきり落ち着きました。血液の濃さが変わる前です。
口やのどを水が通ったことを、脳が「先回り」して受け取っているようです。
ただしマウスの研究で、人の「渇いた感じ」とどう対応するのかは、まだ研究の途中です。

■ 今日からできる、ひとつのこと
研究から言えそうなのは、「決まった量を気にするより、条件で考える」ことです。
・食事の水分も、勘定に入れる
・暑い日、汗をかいた日、運動した日は、増やす
・持病で水分の量を指示されている人は、その指示を優先する
年をとると、のどの渇きを感じにくくなる人もいる、という報告もあります。個人差は大きいそうです。

そしてもう一つ。「飲むかどうか」は、手間でも変わるようです。
2015年、米国ボストンの公立校10校で試験がありました(ケニーら、米国公衆衛生学会誌)。
半分の学校で、食堂の水飲み場の横に紙コップを置き、「水を飲もう」の掲示を貼りました。
3週間後、昼食で水を飲む生徒の割合は、約6%から約13%に増えました。
何もしなかった学校では、約19%から約17%で、増えていません。
対象は子どもの昼食時だけです。コップと掲示のどちらが効いたのかも、分けられていません。
それでも「手を伸ばせば、すぐ飲める」が大事、というのは、大人の机の上でも使えそうな考え方です。

―― ここからは研究とは別の、道具の話です ――
(水筒は医療機器ではありません。病気の予防や、健康への効果をうたうものではありません)

■ Owala(オワラ)FreeSip トライタン 740mL
米国生まれのボトルブランドです。人気の中心は、ステンレス製の「FreeSip(フリーシップ)」。
2020年ごろ、コロナ禍で働く看護師たちの投稿から知られ始めました。
2023年半ばからはTikTokで、米国の10代後半〜20代、特に大学生くらいの若い女性の間で一気に広まりました。
#owala の動画は、累計2億7,200万回再生(メーカー発表)。
国内では2026年2月から正規販売が始まり、雑貨店PLAZAの店頭にも並んでいます。
今回のトライタン版は、その飲み口を、軽いプラスチックの本体に載せたモデルです。

先に、弱点を書きます。
・保冷・保温はできません。氷は早めに溶け、暑い日は外側に水滴がつきます
・熱い飲み物と炭酸は入れられません
・フタまわり(ストロー・パッキン)は、分解して洗い、乾かす手間があります
・透明なぶん、すり傷が目立ちます

それでも、良いところがはっきりしています。
・空の重さが約180g。ステンレスの二重構造をやめ、トライタンという丈夫なプラスチックにしたからです。同じブランドのステンレス版(710mL)は約390gなので、半分以下。通勤のバッグに入れっぱなしにしても、肩が気になりにくい重さです。
・飲み口ひとつで、2通りに飲めます。立てたまま吸えばストロー、傾ければ直飲み。フタやパーツを付け替える必要はありません。パソコン作業中は画面から目を離さずにストローで一口、ジムの後は傾けてごくごく、が同じボトルでできます。
・フタはボタンひとつで開き、持ち手の輪っかがロックを兼ねます。国内のレビューには「バッグに入れる時はロックがかかり、使う時はロックが持ち手代わりになる」という声がありました。
・ストロー付きのタンブラーと違い、飲み口がフタで覆われます。持ち歩く間、口をつける部分がむき出しになりません。
・口が広いので、氷が入れやすく、ブラシも底まで届きます。

ほかにも「ストローのみ、ぐい呑み、選べて飲める!」「ドライブで揺れているときも飲めて良い」という声がありました。
口紅が落ちにくいから、とストロー側を使っている人もいます。

ストローだけの水筒は、ごくごく飲みたいときに物足りない。
直飲みだけの水筒は、作業中に傾けるのがちょっと面倒。
この2つを、フタ一つで解決しようとした設計です。
ストロータイプの定番Stanley(スタンレー)のタンブラーは車やデスク向きですが、飲み口を覆ってロックできる点では、こちらが持ち歩き向きです。

向いているのは、机に向かう時間が長い人、ジムやヨガに通う人、とにかく軽さを優先したい人です。
向かないのは、夏の屋外で冷たさを長く保ちたい人、フタの手入れをしたくない人。その場合は、同じFreeSipのステンレス版のほうが合っています。

たとえば今、午後にはぬるくなったペットボトルを、カバンの奥に入れっぱなしにしていませんか。
これを机の端に置いておくと、ボタンを押してストローで一口、が画面を見たままできます。
透明なので、夕方には「今日はここまで減った」が目で分かります。
飲んだ量を、アプリの数字ではなく、見た目でつかめる。そんな小さな変化です。

フタを替えずに、ストローと直飲みを切り替えられる。それを180gのボトルでできるのが、この一本を選ぶ理由です。気になったら👇

―――

"Drink 2 liters of water a day." The 1945 document often blamed for that advice actually had one more sentence:
"Most of this quantity is contained in prepared foods." 💧
Here's what research says about how much water we really need, and at the end, a bottle built for drinking in small, frequent sips.

■ Where did "8 glasses" come from?
In English it's often called "8×8": eight 8-ounce glasses a day, about 1.9 liters.
In 2002, the American physiologist Heinz Valtin went looking for the evidence behind it. He searched old literature and asked nutrition experts.
His conclusion: he found no scientific studies supporting "at least eight glasses."
That conclusion was about healthy adults living in a temperate climate and spending most of the day sitting.

One likely origin he discussed was a 1945 recommendation from the US Food and Nutrition Board:
"A suitable allowance of water for adults is 2.5 liters daily in most instances."
And then: "Most of this quantity is contained in prepared foods."
One idea is that the last sentence got overlooked, turning a statement about total water into a statement about drinking water.
That's a hypothesis, not settled history.
Valtin also noted that hot weather, hard exercise and some medical conditions can call for more.

■ Measuring the water flowing through 5,604 people
So how much water actually moves through a human body each day?
In 2022, a large study in Science tackled this (Yamada et al.). It was led by a Japanese first author within an international team.
They pooled data from 5,604 people in 23 countries, aged 8 days to 96 years.

The method is neat. Participants drink a small amount of "labeled" water containing deuterium, a slightly heavier form of hydrogen.
By tracking how fast that label leaves the body (through urine and other samples), researchers can work out how much of the body's water is replaced each day.
That's called "water turnover."

One important caveat: water turnover is not how much you drink.
It also includes water in food and the water your body makes when it burns nutrients.

The headline finding: it varies a lot from person to person.
In one example from the paper, a 20-year-old, 70 kg man with typical activity is predicted to turn over about 3.2 liters a day.
A 60 kg woman under the same conditions: about 2.7 liters.
(Those predictions assume an average temperature of 10°C, a country with a high Human Development Index, and a non-athlete.)
Make that 20-year-old an athlete living somewhere hot and humid at 2,000 m altitude, and the prediction climbs to roughly 7 liters.
Body size, activity, temperature, humidity and age all move the number substantially.

That said, this is an observational study that compares many people to find patterns.
The prediction equation explained a bit under half of the differences between individuals.
The paper also notes that it could not separate water from food versus drinks.
So these numbers can't simply be turned into "how much you should drink."

■ What about a Japanese diet?
Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare gives an example of a day's water balance. Out of about 2.5 liters in total:
・about 1.2 L from drinks
・about 1.0 L from food
・about 0.3 L made inside the body
The drinking part is roughly two and a half 500 mL bottles. Rice, miso soup and vegetables carry plenty of water too.
That feels quite different from "drink all 2 liters as water," doesn't it?
(This is one illustrative example; individual needs differ.)

■ Has "drink more, be healthier" been proven?
In 2024, Hakam and colleagues in the US reviewed trials that changed how much water people drank (JAMA Network Open).
They included 18 randomized controlled trials, where people are assigned to groups by chance, like drawing lots.
The median trial had just 48 participants. This is a field full of small studies.
Because the trials differed so much in who they studied and what they measured, the authors did not pool the results into a single number.

Consistent-looking results showed up only in narrow situations:
・weight-loss trials in adults with overweight who drank water before meals alongside a low-calorie diet
・preventing kidney stones from coming back in people who had already had one
There was also one trial in women who normally drank little and had repeated bladder infections, where recurrences dropped.
Results for headaches, on the other hand, were mixed.

In short, "everyone benefits from drinking more" hasn't been shown.
Whether it helps depends on who you are and what the goal is. That's where the evidence stands today.

■ Thirst works ahead of time
When you drink, thirst fades almost immediately.
But it takes a while for water to be absorbed from the gut and dilute the blood.
So why do you feel better so fast?

A 2016 mouse study in Nature offers a clue (Zimmerman et al.).
Thirst-promoting neurons in the brain started quieting down from the very first lick of water.
Within a minute they were clearly suppressed, before the blood had changed.
The brain seems to register water passing through the mouth and throat, and respond ahead of time.
This was in mice, though. How it maps onto human feelings of thirst is still being worked out.

■ One thing you can try today
The practical takeaway: rather than chasing a fixed number, think in terms of conditions.
・Count the water in your food
・Drink more on hot days, sweaty days and exercise days
・If a doctor has given you a fluid limit for a health condition, follow that
Some people also report feeling less thirsty as they get older, though this varies a lot between individuals.

And one more thing: whether people drink seems to depend on convenience too.
In 2015, a trial ran in 10 public schools in Boston (Kenney et al., American Journal of Public Health).
Half the schools put paper cups next to the cafeteria water fountains, plus a "drink water" poster.
Three weeks later, the share of students drinking water at lunch rose from about 6% to about 13%.
In schools with no changes, it went from about 19% to about 17%, with no increase.
This was children at lunchtime only, and the study can't tell whether the cups or the posters did the work.
Still, "water within arm's reach" is an idea that seems worth borrowing for an adult's desk.

―― From here on, it's about a product, separate from the research ――
(A water bottle is not a medical device and makes no claims about preventing disease or improving health.)

■ Owala FreeSip Tritan 740 mL (25 oz)
Owala is an American bottle brand. Its best-known product is the stainless-steel FreeSip.
It first caught on around 2020, through posts by nurses working during the pandemic.
From mid-2023 it took off on TikTok among Gen Z in the US, especially young women around college age.
The brand says #owala videos have passed 272 million views.
Official sales in Japan began in February 2026, and it's now on the shelves at PLAZA variety stores.
This Tritan version puts the same lid on a light plastic body.

First, the downsides:
・No insulation. Ice melts faster, and on hot days the outside gets wet with condensation
・No hot drinks and no carbonated drinks
・The lid area (straw and gasket) needs to be taken apart, washed and dried
・The clear body shows scratches

Now the strengths, and they're clear:
・About 180 g empty. That's because it drops the double-walled steel for Tritan, a tough plastic. The brand's own stainless 710 mL version weighs about 390 g, so this is less than half. You can leave it in a commuter bag and barely notice it on your shoulder.
・One spout, two ways to drink. Keep it upright and sip through the built-in straw, or tilt it and drink straight from the wide opening. No swapping lids or parts. Sip without taking your eyes off your screen while you work, then tilt it back for big gulps after the gym, all with the same bottle.
・The lid flips open with one button, and the carry loop doubles as a lock. One Japanese reviewer wrote that it locks when it goes in the bag, and the lock works as a handle when it's in use.
・Unlike straw tumblers, the spout is covered by the lid. The part you drink from isn't exposed while you carry it.
・The wide mouth makes it easy to add ice, and a brush reaches the bottom.

Other reviewers wrote, "Straw or big gulps, you get to choose!" and "Easy to drink from even on a bumpy drive." One person mentioned using the straw side because it's easier on lipstick.

Straw-only bottles feel limiting when you want a big drink.
Drink-from-the-top bottles are a little awkward to tip while you're working.
This design tries to solve both with one lid.
Stanley's popular straw tumbler shines in the car or on a desk, but for carrying around, the covered, lockable spout here makes more sense.

It suits people who spend long hours at a desk, go to the gym or yoga, or simply want the lightest option.
It's not for people who want drinks to stay cold outdoors in summer, or who don't want to clean a lid. For them, the stainless FreeSip is the better match.

Picture this: right now, maybe there's a lukewarm plastic bottle sitting at the bottom of your bag by mid-afternoon.
Put this one at the corner of your desk instead, press the button, and take a sip through the straw without looking away from your screen.
Because it's clear, by evening you can see exactly how far down it's gone today.
You get a sense of how much you drank from a glance, not from an app. It's a small change.

Straw or straight sip, without changing lids, in a 180 g bottle: that's the reason to pick this one. Take a look 👇

text:
🚨Ninth Circuit grants temporary stay, pausing order that reinstated Roger Rogoff as Western Washington U.S. attorney, for now

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit on Sunday granted the DOJ an administrative stay, pausing a district court order that had blocked President Donald J Trump’s firing of Roger Rogoff and restored him as U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington.

The order, issued by Clerk of Court Molly C. Dwyer, states that the court received the government’s emergency motion for a stay pending appeal and that “the request for an administrative stay is GRANTED.” It adds that the stay “is only intended to preserve the status quo until the substantive motion for a stay pending appeal can be considered on the merits, and does not constitute in any way a decision as to the merits” of the appeal. It was not an en banc ruling and was not signed by a panel of judges.

The stay means Rogoff remains out of the office for now and not a decision on whether President Trump had the power to remove a court-appointed interim U.S. attorney. The Ninth Circuit will next consider the DOJ’s full request for a stay pending appeal; the underlying appeal remains active.

Sunday's stay follows an October 1 ruling by U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian, a Barack Obama appointee and chief judge of the Eastern District of Washington. Speaking from the bench, Bastian granted Rogoff a preliminary injunction, refused to pause it himself, and said Rogoff “is the United States Attorney for the Western District of Washington and has been the rightful holder of that office since July 15, 2026,” the day he took the oath.

The judges of the Western District appointed Rogoff unanimously after the post sat without a Senate-confirmed leader. Federal law lets the attorney general name an interim U.S. attorney for 120 days; once that window closes, the district court may fill the vacancy until the Senate confirms a nominee. Rogoff, a former federal prosecutor and King County Superior Court judge, was sworn in at the Seattle courthouse on the morning of July 15. Trump fired him by email less than an hour later.

The administration had left the office in the hands of Charles Neil Floyd, who had served as interim U.S. attorney and then as first assistant after his statutory term expired. Trump later nominated Pete Serrano, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Eastern Washington and a former Pasco mayor, for the Western District post. Serrano has not been confirmed. Bastian said neither Floyd nor Serrano held the office under his injunction.

Rogoff sued in July, arguing the firing sidestepped the Senate’s confirmation role. Bastian on Oct. 1 agreed, stating Congress did not give the power to fill the office to the president alone and that allowing the removal “would upend the framework created by the Constitution and the statutes.” 

Bastian's district court order—which is now stayed after Sunday's decision—had barred the Trump administration from carrying out the firing, treating Rogoff as removed, or blocking his access to the office, staff and pay, and had entitled him to back pay. 

@WAGOP Chairman Jim Walsh, interviewed by the Lynnwood Times Sunday evening after the stay, described Bastian’s ruling as “patently illegal” and said the Ninth Circuit’s weekend stay correctly held that a president can fire a U.S. attorney.

He called the Senate blue-slip practice that Sen. @PattyMurray has used against Serrano an “arcane U.S. Senate policy, not law.” He said it is a courtesy that lets home-state senators “blackball” a nominee. 

After Sens. Murray and @SenatorCantwell blocked Serrano’s earlier path to confirmation as U.S. attorney for the Eastern District—it was mostly Murray—the DOJ found a workaround by naming Serrano first assistant and a special adviser to the U.S. attorney general effectively managing the Spokane AG's Office without the formal title.

Asked why Sen. Murray continues to hold up Serrano's appointment, @JimWalshLD19 said fraud investigations are “what Senator Murray’s worried about” and that she “may be implicated” indirectly because she has supported programs now subject to fraud allegations. 

Walsh clarified that he is not claiming Sen. Murray was “caught red-handed, fraudulently stuffing $100 bills into her freezer,” but that she is attached by backing those programs. 

The example he shared with the Lynnwood Times was Apple Health Medicaid benefits for illegal aliens: he said Washington may offer state benefits, but federal money cannot be used, and that there are “rumors and allegations” that the state's Health Care Authority has commingled federal funds in a way that would violate federal law. Walsh added that these matters are under investigation. 

Walsh said he does not expect the case to reach the Supreme Court but suspects the Ninth Circuit will reject the district court’s opinion and that the Supreme Court will decline review. He said he talks with Serrano often but had not spoken with him about Sunday's Ninth Circuit stay. 

Serrano, Walsh said, “has nothing to do with” the Rogoff firing by President Trump and is not as directly involved in the process with Rogoff.

text:
BREAKING📡| #Iran's Oil Minister Resigns As #Tehran Loads No Barrels of #Oil for a Month

Mohsen Paknejad resigned Sunday after serving as oil minister since August 2024, replaced by Hamid Bovard, CEO of the National Iranian Oil Company, as acting minister. 

The official line from the president's office states "Personal reasons." 

A resignation #Paknejad had apparently offered before, which Pezeshkian initially declined, before ultimately accepting it "at Paknejad's insistence."

Bloomberg reported this same week that Iran loaded zero crude oil onto tankers in September, the first full month of zero exports since the US-Israeli war began February 28, down from roughly 250,000 barrels/day in August alone. 

That's not a gradual decline, it's a total collapse in a single month, which would contribute to Iranian leadership pressuring the oil minister leading to his resignation.

There's also a specific controversy the Iranian Journalists Club flagged as overtaking Paknejad's final weeks in office which was a cancellation of a contract to sell oil to seven Chinese refineries, China being Iran's primary remaining crude buyer throughout this war. 

Losing that outlet, on top of the US naval blockade, would explain a lot more than "personal reasons" ever could.

Paknejad told state media "revenues of the oil that we have sold are still coming and that will continue, God willing," a statement that aged within days against the zero-export data.

His replacement isn't a political outsider.

Hamid #Bovard has spent his career in oilfield operations (National Iranian South Oil Company, Marun Oil and Gas), and the US Treasury already sanctioned him directly back in February 2025 under Executive Order 13902 specifically for his role funding "Iran's regional military activities and the IRGC-Qods Force." 

Iran just handed its oil ministry to someone Washington has already formally designated as a financier of its proxy network, not exactly a conciliatory signal.

Whether Paknejad actually left for personal reasons or was pushed out over a collapsing export pipeline and a canceled China deal, the timing, zero barrels loaded, a sanctioned successor stepping in, and an intensifying US financial pressure campaign no longer matters. 

Iran's crude oil is at its most instable point and the next President has a full plate ahead of him.
