🚩The war that shattered Iraq

(An insightful article on Military intervention of USA  in Iraq  & it's withdrawl .The 2003 invasion was justified through the claim that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction and represented an urgent danger. The weapons were not found.
USA came, ruined ,and  handed Iraqis  back to the same old enemies.  Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that the post-9/11 wars produced between 4.5 million and 4.7 million direct and indirect deaths and displaced more than 38 million people. Iraq remains the clearest example of how quickly the promise of security can become a prolonged political and human disaster.But the deeper failure was the inability to translate battlefield victories into political institutions capable of surviving without foreign military power. As Masrour foreign military power. Barzani, whose Kurdistan Regional Government governs Iraq's Kurdish-majority north, described the US withdrawal from Iraq as "shameful" )

This is how a war supposedly fought for security can end: with a country left carrying the con-sequences long after the soldiers who invaded it have gone.
Twenty-five years after September 11, 2001, the American-led wars in Afghanistan and Iraq offer a record of military intervention that is impossible to separate from the destruction of institutions, displacement, sectarian violence and the weakening of societies supposedly being protected. Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that the post-9/11 wars produced between 4.5 million and 4.7 million direct and indirect deaths and displaced more than 38 million people. Iraq remains the clearest example of how quickly the promise of security can become a prolonged political and human disaster.

The 2003 invasion was justified through the claim that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction and represented an urgent danger. The weapons were not found. The Iraq Survey Group did not discover an active Iraqi WMD stock-pile, while later official investiga-tions exposed serious failures in the intelligence used to support the pre-war case. Saddam's dicta-torship and his previous use of chemical weapons were real. What collapsed was the proposi-tion that Iraq possessed the active WMD capability used to justify the invasion. Yet the war went ahead, and the United States then faced the far more difficult question of what would replace the state it had destroyed. The occupation did not simply remove Saddam Hussein while preserving Iraq's governmental machinery. Coalition Provisional Authority Order No. 1 imposed sweeping de Ba'athification, while Order No. 2 dis-solved the Iraqi military and other state institutions. These were occupation deci sions, not inevitable consequences of removing Saddam. The dissolution of the army was especially consequential. Hundreds of thousands of trained person-nel suddenly lost employment, authority and their place in the new state. Not all had been committed Ba'athists. Many had joined the army as a profession. Removing the institution therefore did not eliminate military knowledge or political grievances. It scattered them into a country already filled with weapons, uncertainty and anger. Former soldiers, Ba'athists, nationalists, Islamists, criminals and foreign jihadists became part of an expanding insurgency.

Sunni resistance and al-Qaeda in Iraq grew amid the disorder, while sectarian militias expanded. The bombing of the al Askari shrine in Samarra in 2006 helped unleash an extraordinary escalation of Sunni-Shia violence, turning Baghdad into a city of checkpoints, kidnappings, assas-sinations and death squads. The occupa tion had dismantled one of the state's prin cipal instruments of order without ing a credible substitute.

The United States changed strategy. The 2007 surge, the Sunni Awakening and changes in military tactics reduced vio-lence, but they did not create a durable political settlement. Sunni tribes that had fought al-Qaeda alongside American forces later felt marginalised by the government in Baghdad, creating grievances that were exploited by the organisation that evolved into Islamic State. It would be simplistic to say that America direct ly created ISIS. Its rise also depended on the Syrian civil war, the col lapse of Syrian state authority, sectarian pol-itics and decisions by Iraqi and Syrian actors. But the chain linking the 2003 invasion, the destruction of Iraqi insti-tutions, the insurgency, al-Qaeda in Iraq and the later rise of Islamic State is part of the document ed history of the organisation. The irony is brutal. America invaded partly in the name of preventing terrorism, fought an insurgency that produced al-Qaeda in Iraq, later returned to fight the organi-sation that emerged from that move ment, and ultimately fought Islamic State in a country whose political order its own invasion had helped destroy.

The human cost extended beyond the battlefields. On 19 November 2005, after a US Marine was killed by a roadside bomb at Haditha, Marines killed 24 Iraqi civilians, including women and children. The initial account did not accurately describe what had happened, and subse quent investigations produced criminal proceedings with varying outcomes. Abu Ghraib exposed an even wider crisis of detention, abuse and accountability. Photographs of prisoners being humiliat possessed became symbols of an occupation that claimed to be constructing a democratic order. Reconstruction brought another contra-diction. The Coalition Provisional Authority controlled approximately $23 billion in Iraqi revenues and assets between May 2003 and June 2004, while the United States separate ly appropriated billions for reconstruction and security. The evidence does not support the crude claim that America simply stole Iraq's oil, but the occupying authority exercised extraordinary control over a sovereign country's finances while its institutions were being rebuilt. A huge con-tracting system followed, involving con struction, logistics, security and mainte-nance, with oversight struggling to keep pace with enormous spending. The result was an economy dependent on oil and foreign-supported reconstruction. The World Bank estimates that in 2025, oil p-resented about 53 per cent of real GDF 88 per cent of government revenue and 91er cent of merchandise exports.

The consequences reached far beyond government accounts. The World Bank its Iraqi unemployment at about 15.5 er cent in 2025 and identifies youth empoy-ment as a major structural challenge, while women remain dramatically under-represented in the labour force. UNICEF says close to 3.2 million Iraqi school-age children are out of school and links the edu cational crisis to decades of conflict and under-investment. More than one million Iraqis remained internally displaced years after the territorial defeat of Islamic State.

The fact, however, is that Saddam's Iraq had been a hostile barrier to Iranian regional influence. Its destruction removed that barrier, allowing political parties, reli-gious networks and armed groups connect-ed to Iran to become deeply embedded in the post-Saddam system. Some militias that fought American forces eventually became part of Iraq's political and security architec ture. Washington therefore removed an enemy of Iran and spent years confronting forces that benefited from the new order.

But the deeper failure was the inability to translate battlefield victories into political institutions capable of surviving without foreign military power. As Masrour foreign military power. Barzani, whose Kurdistan Regional Government governs Iraq's Kurdish-major-ity north, described the US withdrawal from Iraq as "shameful".

The writer is columnist based in Colombo

📌 The Hidden Opportunity in Long-Term Bonds: Should You Buy the $Apple 2060 Bond?

🚨 What Happened?

Corporate bonds with ultra-long durations issued during the low-interest-rate era (2020–2021) continue to trade at massive discounts. Apple’s bond maturing in August 2060 (carrying a 2.55% coupon) currently trades around $47 to $50, delivering a Yield to Maturity (YTM) of approximately 6.0% to 6.3%.

🔍 The Breakdown

🎯 The Key Point: Buying a bond with a $100 par value for roughly $48 means that a significant portion of your total return doesn’t just come from the annual coupon, but from the capital appreciation (often tax-advantaged depending on your jurisdiction) realized when the bond is redeemed at par in 2060.

💡 Why It Matters: You lock in an annualized return of roughly 6% backed by one of the strongest balance sheets in corporate history (Apple), while capturing explosive price asymmetry if macroeconomic benchmark rates drop structurally in the coming decades (due to duration sensitivity).

🎒 Concept Check: "Duration" measures how sensitive a bond’s price is to changes in interest rates. The longer the maturity, the more violently the price reacts: if interest rates fall, ultra-long-duration bonds soar in value much faster than short-term paper.
💡 Hidden Risks & The Ideal Investor Profile

The Volatility Trap (Duration Risk): With a maturity spanning over 30 years, if inflation persists or interest rates continue to climb higher, the market price of this $48 bond can drop further in the short term. This instrument is strictly reserved for investors who can (and will) hold the asset all the way to maturity in 2060.

Equivalent Alternatives: Other tech giants (Microsoft, Alphabet), defensive staples (Johnson & Johnson, Procter & Gamble), and 30-year U.S. Treasuries offer similar deep-discount profiles for investors looking to diversify corporate credit risk.

📌 Geopolitics and Semiconductors: What the Delayed Taiwan Risk Means for AI Infrastructure

🚨 What Happened?

U.S. intelligence and defense officials have indicated to Reuters that a direct Chinese military invasion of Taiwan before 2028 is increasingly unlikely. While Beijing's objective for the People's Liberation Army to be "ready" by 2027 (marking the military's 100th anniversary) remains intact, military readiness does not equal an invasion order.

Furthermore, Beijing is closely watching Taiwan's pivotal 2028 presidential election. If the incumbent pro-sovereignty party retains power, strategists suggest the geopolitical tension could escalate rapidly around that window. Effectively, the immediate "2027 scare" timeline has slid, granting the global technology supply chain roughly two additional years of uninterrupted baseline production.

🔍 The Breakdown

🎯 The Main Event: Rather than an imminent military confrontation, the near-term risk curve has flattened. Internal military purges within the PLA and strategic patience regarding Taiwan's political evolution push the critical window out toward the late 2020s.

💡 Why It Matters for AI (TSMC's Crucial Role): TSMC remains the undisputed lifeblood of advanced semiconductor manufacturing. Leading-edge AI chips powering Nvidia, Broadcom, and custom automotive silicon are overwhelmingly fabricated on Taiwanese soil. While foundry expansions in Arizona represent vital regional diversification, they remain a fractional slice rather than a complete, independent mirror of TSMC’s massive output.

🎒 Concept Check ("Geopolitical Concentration Risk"): This occurs when a critical global industry relies heavily on a single geographic choke point. When the timeline for potential disruption is pushed back, the immediate risk premium embedded in semiconductor-heavy equities compresses, allowing uninterrupted revenue generation to compound in the interim.

💡 Strategic Takeaways & Mitigation

The Race to 2028 (The "Terafab" Horizon): Two additional years of stable production provide crucial runway for alternative manufacturing ecosystems to scale. Few Saints have aroused so much admiration and enthusiasm immediately after their death; few have acquired a more astonishing popularity everywhere on earth; few have been so rapidly raised to the altars as was this holy young Carmelite. Marie Françoise Thérèse Martin, known as the Little Flower of Jesus, was born January 2, 1873 at Alençon in Normandy, France, of very Christian parents. The Martins, who lost four of their little ones in early infancy or childhood, regarded their children as gifts from heaven and offered them to God before their birth. Thérèse was the last flower of this blessed stem, which gave four Sisters to the Carmel of Lisieux, still another to the Visitation of Caen. The five sisters were left without their mother, a victim of cancer, when Thérèse was only four years old; but her two oldest sisters were of an age to take excellent care of the household and continue the Christian character formation of the younger ones, which their mother had initiated. Their saintly father was soon to see his little flock separated, however, when one after the other they left to enter religious life. He blessed each one and gave them all back to God, with humble gratitude to God for having chosen his daughters.
.
From childhood Thérèse had manifested a tender piety which her naturally lively temperament could not alter. Her mother's death affected her profoundly, however, and at the age of nine she was visited with a severe trial in the form of an illness the doctors could not diagnose, and which seemed incurable. She was instantly restored to her ordinary good health by the Virgin Mary, in answer to her desolate sisters' prayers; Thérèse saw Her statue become animated, to smile at her with an ineffable tenderness as she lay on her bed of suffering.
.
Before the age of fifteen Thérèse already desired to enter the Carmel of Lisieux, where her two eldest sisters were already nuns; a trip to Rome and a petition at the knees of the Holy Father Leo XIII gave her the inalterable answer that her Superiors would regulate the matter. Many prayers finally obtained an affirmative reply to her ardent request, and four months after her fifteenth birthday she entered Carmel with an ineffable joy. She could say then, I no longer have any desire but to love Jesus even to folly.
.
She adopted flowers as the symbol of her love for her Divine Spouse and offered all her little daily sacrifices and works as rose petals at the feet of Jesus. Divine Providence gave to the world the autobiography of this true Saint, whose little way of spiritual childhood was described in her own words in her Story of a Soul. She could not offer God the macerations of the great soldiers of God, only her desires to love Him as they had loved Him, and to serve Him in every way possible, not only as a cloistered nun, but as a missionary, a priest, a hero of the faith, a martyr. She chose all in spirit, for her beloved Lord. Later she would be named patroness of missions. Her spirituality does not imply only sweetness and light, however; this loving child of God passed by a tunnel of desolate spiritual darkness, yet never ceased to smile at Him, wanting to serve Him, if it were possible, without His even knowing it.
When nine years had passed in the Carmel, the little flower was ready to be plucked for heaven; and in a slow agony of consumption, Thérèse made her final offering to God. She suffered so severely that she said she would never have believed it possible, and could only explain it by her desire to save souls for God. text:
Recently traveled abroad. It opened my eyes to a world of business people, many who lived in the United States, and others who benefit from stocks in the United States while living abroad. 

Egypt was built off the backs of laborers like you and me but Pharaohs, left the legacy. Sounds familiar? History is cyclical. 

Egypt was the influencer then, the United states is now. Brief history of Egypt and how much people in power have lied: 

Egypt is one of the oldest continuous civilizations, and later cultures borrowed from it: stone monuments, a divine king backed by bureaucracy, an afterlife religion, a civil calendar, and a reputation for craft and engineering. Greeks and Romans absorbed pieces of that, and the Bible is partly set against an Egyptian backdrop. It is an early ancestor, not the template.

Powerful local rulers first unified the Nile by conquest and control of irrigation and trade. Once the state existed, kingship became hereditary and was wrapped in religion: the king as Horus on earth, later also son of Re. The word “pharaoh” began as the palace (“great house”) and only later stuck to the man. Coups, civil wars, and foreign takeovers still happened.

Other strands mattered as much. Mesopotamia shared sacred monarchy and big-state religion. Israel offered one God, covenant, and law as moral constitution. Greece contributed citizenship, debate, and political philosophy. Rome contributed law, administration, and republic-then-empire institutions. Europe inherited the mix; Christianity carried and reshaped it.

Rulers who hold the army and the treasury usually set the official gods and rituals. Beliefs also move through conquest, writing, and new claims that answer fear and meaning. Shared worries—death, order, a just cosmos—persist. Those rituals were a machine for them.

An afterlife never stopped brutality. Pharaohs who built a huge afterlife religion still used forced labor and violence; later kings who believed in heaven and hell still fought wars. Belief or unbelief does not, by itself, explain why elites use ideology to justify order and their own place. Fear of death often makes people grab control.

Power is the ability to decide who eats, who is safe, whose name lasts, whose children inherit. For a pharaoh that meant the Nile, the army, the temples, and the story that the world would fall apart without him. The content changes; the prize does not: not being at someone else’s mercy.

Unification is rarely a meeting of equals. Egypt was unified by conquest, then held by a court claiming divine right. Once one side wins, force and threat keep the loser from trying again. Ideology—afterlife, ma’at, nation, security—then calls the force necessary order. Violence is the old, cheap tool for making other people stop.

Power answers several fears at once: annihilation, humiliation, chaos, being forgotten. A tomb and a title both say “I was here.” Unification sounds clean until the question is whose terms, whose god, whose law, whose surplus. Those on top call their position the peace; those underneath call it domination.

Believing you live forever can justify harsh rule (“I keep the cosmos”). Believing you do not can do the same (“this life is all I get”). Neither reliably produces peace. What reduces raw violence over time is rival power, law that binds the ruler too, and institutions that make cooperation safer than the next war.

The core fear is real. Power is the attempt to master that fear by mastering other people. Unification, when it happens, is usually the peace that follows a win, not the alternative to wanting to win.

Moral of the story?  You are your own creator. Live your life. Is short.

text:
Sjoe! 😳 Somebody Left Half the History Book at Home ~ 🗺️ What Happens When an Entire Chapter of History Goes Missing? The Price of an Incomplete Map: History, Influence and South Africa’s Strategic Choices 🇿🇦🗺️
South Africa is still navigating by maps that leave entire continents blank.
The same criteria used to name European overseas expansion as colonial—territorial conquest, hierarchical rule, demographic change, long-duration slave systems—are present in the Islamic expansions that began after 632 CE and stretched within a century from Spain to the borders of India. 

The eastern slave trades that accompanied them moved an estimated ten to eighteen million Africans across the Sahara, Red Sea and Indian Ocean, lasting more than a thousand years (Lovejoy, 2012; Segal, 2001). The vocabulary applied to these facts is not the same. Modern curricula, activist language and much commentary apply the full lexicon of conquest and oppression far more consistently to post-1500 Western cases while framing the earlier expansions as organic diffusion or cultural flowering.

This is not a minor academic preference. It is a systematic filter that shapes education, risk assessment and foreign policy. 

Identical categories of human behaviour receive radically different moral treatment depending on the civilisational source. Incomplete maps produce incomplete judgement.

That is the claim. The evidence that follows tests it from history, diplomacy, institutional funding, cognitive labelling and institutional survival. 

The argument is falsifiable: new primary evidence showing the eastern trades were marginal, that classical jurisprudence lacks hierarchical content, that South African voting patterns are randomly distributed, or that organisational density has no agenda-setting effect would weaken it. 

No such contradictory evidence currently outweighs the cumulative record.

1. The Missing Continents

After the death of Muhammad, Arab-Muslim armies dismantled the Sassanid Empire, seized the Levant and Egypt from the Byzantines, swept across North Africa, crossed into Spain in 711, and later pushed deep into the Indian subcontinent. Contemporary chronicles record the systematic installation of new rulers, the institutionalisation of dhimmi status, and the destruction or conversion of religious sites in many locales. 

The eastern slave trades that accompanied these expansions formed integral economic systems lasting far longer than the Atlantic trade (Lovejoy, 2012; Segal, 2001).

European colonial expansion after 1500 receives the full contemporary vocabulary of colonisation and moral condemnation. Parallel Islamic imperial projects are more often presented as background conditions. Post-colonial frameworks have reinforced the asymmetry by prioritising Western agency and guilt while treating non-Western imperial agency as secondary. 

Academic and activist careers are rarely advanced by emphasising non-Western imperial violence with equal force. Funding streams, publication norms and social prestige reward narratives that keep the moral spotlight fixed on the West.

South African education largely inherited this map. Residual liberation mythology treats the Western record as uniquely requiring continuous scrutiny while the parallel record remains largely exempt. 

The practical result is a generation of students and policymakers trained to recognise one set of patterns with high resolution and another with deliberate soft focus. Pattern recognition suffers. 

Policy that cannot name parallel incentives cannot evaluate them.

The 1996 Constitution rests on the premise that equal standards under law are possible and that citizens can reason together from shared facts. Incomplete historical maps quietly undermine that premise by training different groups to inhabit different factual universes before they ever reach the statute book. 

When school history presents one set of conquests as uniquely requiring perpetual moral excavation and another as cultural background, the civic foundation itself is uneven. The unintended consequence is a public square in which some patterns are treated as self-evident while identical patterns elsewhere remain almost unspeakable.

Sjoe!
It is remarkable how efficiently a moral vocabulary can develop selective amnesia when the alternative would require redrawing the approved map.

Questions Stirring:
Why do identical factual criteria of territorial conquest, demographic change and institutional hierarchy produce opposite linguistic outcomes?
Why has educational language largely exempted one set of empires?
What happens to public judgement when large continents of the historical record remain faint?

What these questions together reveal:
Together they expose the cost of incomplete maps: societies that cannot name parallel patterns across civilisations lose the capacity to evaluate risk and continuity with clear eyes. The questions matter because education that filters the past produces policy that filters the present, and a constitutional order built on equal standards cannot long survive unequal factual foundations.

2. When Solidarity Overrides Interest

After 1994 the African National Congress translated liberation-era anti-imperial solidarity into durable diplomatic alignment with the Islamic Republic of Iran. Successive governments defended Iran’s nuclear programme at the IAEA, abstained or opposed United Nations resolutions on Iranian human-rights abuses, hosted high-level military and political visits, and facilitated commercial links. 

Iran’s admission into the BRICS process during South Africa’s chairmanship and Pretoria’s decision to initiate the 2023 International Court of Justice case against Israel further illustrate the pattern.

Muslims constitute roughly 1.5–3 percent of South Africa’s population. Organised advocacy networks and residual ANC ideological narratives have nevertheless amplified influence inside foreign-policy institutions. The outcome is marked selectivity: intense legal and rhetorical focus on one conflict coincides with muted responses to Iranian domestic repression and regional proxy activity. 

Western partners have registered the costs through aid reviews and trade friction.

Historical solidarity has, in measurable ways, overridden contemporary national-interest calculations. Liberation mythology retains high political value inside the governing party long after the original struggle ended. 

Aligning with states that frame themselves as anti-imperial offers symbolic continuity at relatively low immediate domestic cost, even when the long-term diplomatic and economic price is higher. 

The filter becomes self-reinforcing: each new act of solidarity strengthens the narrative that justifies the next.

In a constitutional democracy the foreign-policy machinery is meant to serve the permanent interests of the state, not the temporary emotional satisfaction of a historical narrative. When the narrative becomes the filter, trade-offs are no longer weighed; they are pre-decided. 

Opportunity costs accumulate quietly: potential investment, technology partnerships, and security cooperation with partners who share liberal institutional norms are discounted because they do not fit the preferred story. Over time the country pays in reduced strategic flexibility and diminished ability to extract concessions from any side.

Sjoe!
It is a peculiar form of strategic clarity that can detect every alleged injustice in one direction while developing progressive myopia in the other.

Questions Stirring:
How does a liberation narrative become a permanent foreign-policy filter decades after the original struggle ended?
Why does intense scrutiny of one conflict coexist with relative silence on the internal conduct of a key partner?
What are the long-term diplomatic and economic costs of subordinating national interest to residual ideology?

What these questions together reveal:
Together they show that foreign policy is not theatre. When historical narrative consistently overrides measurable national interest, the country pays in influence, investment and strategic flexibility. The questions matter because a democracy that cannot update its alliances on evidence eventually loses the ability to protect its own citizens’ material interests in a multipolar world.

3. The Soft-Power Purchase

Qatar has transferred very large sums—running into the billions—into American universities through Education City campuses and related gifts. Northwestern, Georgetown, Cornell, Carnegie Mellon and Texas A&M are among the recipients. Documented contractual arrangements give the funder consultation rights over senior appointments, prior approval over intellectual-property disposition, and governance access through advisory bodies. 

Parallel soft-power channels and organised advocacy networks already operate inside South African universities and policy institutes.

Transparency deficits allow external priorities to set agendas without reciprocal accountability. Funding sources, contractual conditions and intellectual-property leverage must now be subjected to the same rigorous scrutiny previously reserved for colonial legacies. 

Mandatory disclosure regimes and governance safeguards that treat all foreign influence by identical standards are required. Without them, any single narrative can purchase institutional climate. 

The risk is progressive loss of independent analytical capacity precisely where open societies most need clear-eyed evaluation of competing doctrinal and geopolitical incentives.

Universities are not neutral platforms. They are the institutions that train the next generation of officials, journalists and judges. When external funding quietly shapes the questions that may be asked and the answers that are rewarded, the downstream effect appears years later in foreign-policy memos, editorial pages and classroom syllabi. 

Governance systems that treat foreign money as pure generosity while ignoring the accompanying expectations create a structural vulnerability. The same principle that demands scrutiny of domestic political donations ought to apply, without exemption, to large external flows that purchase access to the knowledge-producing centres of the society.

Sjoe!
Demography is not destiny. Organised affinity plus elite access often is.

Questions Stirring:
How do organisational density and elite affinity allow limited demographic weight to shape national posture?
Why do certain framings become protected from scrutiny by social and professional costs?
What does institutional resilience actually require when taboos limit open evaluation of trade-offs?

What these questions together reveal:
Together they demonstrate that democracy is not only about majorities. It is also about whether elites remain willing to test their own narratives against evidence when organised networks press in a single direction. The questions matter because institutional capture rarely announces itself; it arrives as funding, fellowships and the quiet social cost of asking the wrong question.

4. The Silencing Label

Core Islamic sources—the Quran, major Hadith collections and classical jurisprudence—contain extensive material on warfare against non-believers, hierarchical status for non-Muslims, capital penalties for apostasy, and severe restrictions on blasphemy and free inquiry. When large populations treat these texts as authoritative, measurable correlates appear: elevated support for sharia criminal penalties in multiple surveys, higher incidence of Islamist terrorism relative to other religious traditions in post-2001 databases, and persistent gaps in acceptance of liberal norms such as gender equality and free speech (Saad, 2020).

Labelling ordinary pattern recognition of these incentives “Islamophobia” collapses the distinction between ideas and persons. Concern about doctrines is reclassified as a mental disorder. Western institutional reluctance to apply ordinary scrutiny has been described as suicidal empathy: empathy redirected toward ideological outsiders even when reciprocal commitment to open society is low (Saad, 2020). 

The practical effect is diminished capacity for evidence-based policy on integration, speech and security—without requiring collective hostility toward individuals who hold the faith only nominally.

A constitutional order that cannot distinguish between criticising a set of ideas and attacking a group of people has already surrendered the basic tool of liberal self-defence. 

The label functions as a pre-emptive veto on evidence. Once pattern recognition itself is treated as moral failure, the society loses the ability to update on new information. 

Free-speech protections under the South African Constitution become harder to defend when the very act of noticing certain patterns is framed as pathology rather than analysis.

Sjoe!
There is a special kind of intellectual gymnastics required to treat pattern recognition as a clinical condition while treating the patterns themselves as invisible.

Questions Stirring:
When does evidence-based updating about doctrinal incentives become pathologised?
Why is the cognitive distinction between ideas and persons so readily collapsed in this domain?
What institutional costs follow when ordinary risk assessment is treated as moral failure?

What these questions together reveal:
Together they show that societies that cannot distinguish adaptive caution from prejudice lose the tools needed to protect the open institutions they claim to value. The questions matter because a democracy that pathologises its own threat detection eventually loses the ability to notice threats at all.

5. The Survival Condition

Empires, slavery, religious expansion and hierarchical rule appear across civilisations and eras; they are not unique to any single tradition. Applying maximal moral and linguistic severity only to recent Western cases while softening or omitting parallel non-Western episodes generates distorted analytical maps. 

Evolutionary reasoning further suggests that societies which refuse to notice recurring patterns lose predictive accuracy (Karsh, 2006; Saad, 2020).

Consistent standards require evaluating ideas and outcomes on their merits rather than the identity of the actors. Without such even-handedness, liberal societies impair their ability to diagnose genuine risks, support genuine reform within any tradition, and defend the open institutions they claim to value. 

The alternative is selective blindness that privileges narrative coherence over empirical pattern recognition.

The practical consequence is cumulative. Incomplete historical maps produce incomplete risk assessments. Incomplete risk assessments produce policies that are slower to recognise emerging problems and quicker to pathologise those who notice them. 

Over time the society’s capacity for clear-eyed self-preservation erodes.

South Africa’s Constitution assumes that citizens can reason together from shared facts. Incomplete maps quietly revoke that assumption. Generational effects compound the problem: each cohort trained on selective records finds it harder to recognise the selectivity itself. Institutional resilience depends less on formal constitutional text than on the willingness of successive generations to apply the same standards to every record that claims moral authority.

Sjoe!
Universal principles that only travel in one direction are not universal. They are preferences wearing a gown of principle.

Questions Stirring:
Why do identical categories of human behaviour receive radically different moral treatment depending on the source?
What predictive capacity is lost when societies refuse to notice recurring patterns?
How can open institutions be defended if the standards used to evaluate threats are applied unevenly?

What these questions together reveal:
Together they establish that selective standards are not merely academic. They shape education, policy, risk assessment and the long-term viability of the liberal order itself. The questions matter because a constitutional democracy that cannot apply its own standards evenly eventually loses the capacity to defend those standards at all.

Synthesis

Independent lines of evidence—chronicles, demographic estimates, doctrinal texts, survey data, diplomatic voting records and commercial linkages—converge on the same diagnosis. 

The incomplete historical record of Islamic imperial expansion and slave trades, the pathologising of ordinary threat detection, the concrete case of South African foreign-policy alignment with Iran, the mechanism of minority ideological capture, and the broader demand for even-handed standards reinforce one another.

The argument is falsifiable. New primary evidence showing that the eastern slave trades were marginal, that classical jurisprudence lacks hierarchical content, that South African UN voting patterns are randomly distributed, or that organisational density has no agenda-setting effect would weaken the case. 

No such contradictory evidence currently outweighs the cumulative record. The stakes are practical: societies that cannot apply the same criteria to every tradition lose the capacity to assess risk accurately or to defend the liberal order they profess.

Objections

One common objection is that earlier Islamic expansions occurred in a different moral universe and therefore cannot be judged by modern standards. Yet the same objection is rarely extended to European empires of the same pre-modern periods; the filter remains selective.

A second objection holds that concern about doctrinal incentives inevitably slides into collective prejudice against individuals. The distinction between ideas and persons is precisely the safeguard against that slide; collapsing the distinction is what produces the prejudice.

A third objection claims that South Africa’s Iran alignment is simple anti-imperial solidarity with no selective cost. The measurable diplomatic friction with Western partners and the muted response to Iranian internal repression indicate otherwise.

Conclusion

Selective histories produce selective blindness. The record of rapid Islamic imperial expansion, long-duration slave trades, doctrinal incentives for hierarchical rule, and contemporary policy alignments that privilege residual ideology over national interest is not obscure. It is simply filtered.

Restoring the missing continents to the map does not require hostility toward any community. It requires the ordinary intellectual discipline of applying the same standards across civilisations.

South Africa, like every open society, inherits both the gains and the unfinished business of history. The question is whether it will continue to navigate by incomplete maps or whether it will insist on seeing the full terrain. 

The answer will shape not only foreign policy but the clarity with which the country assesses risk, reform and its own liberal commitments.

The converging evidence shows that selective application of historical and moral categories produces distorted maps, impaired pattern recognition and policy choices that privilege narrative over evidence.

Ireland Needs a Foreign Agents Registration Act

A criminal complaint, filed thousands of miles away, ought to make governments elsewhere sit up rather straighter in their chairs.

The FBI has arrested Wanying “Heather” Zhang, a 34-year-old California resident accused of acting as an unregistered agent of the People’s Republic of China and of surveilling the American-based son of Taiwan’s President, Lai Ching-te, and his family.¹

The complaint was filed in the United States District Court for the Central District of California on 3 October 2026. The affidavit was sworn by FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt, and Zhang is accused of violating 18 U.S.C. § 951 — acting in the United States as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the Attorney General.¹

Federal investigators allege that Zhang travelled to Seattle in September 2025 and gathered photographs and other information concerning the Taiwanese President’s son and his family. The allegations remain to be tested in court.¹

But there is a lesson here for Ireland.

Let me be absolutely clear: @MichealMartinTD and his Government have, in my view, taken nothing like the steps necessary to protect Ireland from foreign influence operations — whether they originate with an adversary, an ally or something occupying the diplomatic grey territory in between.

And some uncomfortable questions need to be asked about foreign-linked organisations and individuals operating in Ireland and seeking access to public officials, Government departments and other State bodies.

One example requiring proper scrutiny is Natalia Eismont. When previously contacted, Ms Eismont’s public profile described her as working in Ireland for the Ukrainian Government’s Ombudsman. She now describes herself, rather mysteriously, as a volunteer. 

However, Ms. Eismont continues to use a Ukrainian government email address and is directly associated with an organisation strangely called the Future of Ukrainian Nation in Ireland.

Perhaps I have been mistaken, for I had always understood the Republic of Ireland to contain one sovereign nation, one democratic future and one people to whom that future ultimately belonged — the Irish people.

Ireland may offer friendship abroad, shelter to those in need and cooperation with other governments. But friendship is not ownership, hospitality is not political surrender, and diplomacy is not a licence for another state to shape Ireland’s priorities.

The political future of Ireland should be decided in Ireland, by the Irish people, through Irish democratic institutions, and in the Irish national interest.

That used to be called sovereignty.

One had rather assumed it still was.

That organisation itself says that it was established in Kerry in May 2023 and describes its purpose as representing and supporting Ukrainians living in Ireland and promoting their integration into Irish society.²

There is nothing inherently improper about advocacy, community organisation or lobbying. Ireland itself recognises lobbying as a legitimate part of democratic life.

The question is transparency.

Who is representing whom?

Who is funding whom?

On whose behalf are approaches to Ministers, civil servants and State agencies being made?

And where foreign governments, officials, organisations or interests are involved, what precisely is the relationship?

These are not unreasonable questions in a sovereign democracy. They are elementary ones.

The United States has long attempted to answer them through the Foreign Agents Registration Act — FARA — which requires certain persons acting as agents of foreign principals and engaging in specified political or other activities to disclose publicly their relationship with those foreign principals, together with relevant activities, receipts and expenditure.³

Under FARA, “political activities” include activities intended to influence US Government officials or sections of the American public concerning domestic or foreign policy or the political interests of a foreign government or political party.⁴

Ireland needs to consider its own equivalent.

Ireland already has a Register of Lobbying under the Regulation of Lobbying Act 2015. Its purpose is to make information available concerning the identity of those communicating with designated public officials on particular policy, legislative or prospective Government decisions.⁵

But ordinary lobbying regulation and the national-security problem of foreign-state influence are not necessarily the same thing.

A modern Irish Foreign Agents Registration Act should therefore require those acting politically, publicly or institutionally on behalf of foreign governments and qualifying foreign principals to disclose clearly whom they represent, what work they undertake, what money or material assistance they receive and what contacts they make with Irish public officials.

Sunlight, after all, remains considerably cheaper than counter-intelligence.

Because as matters stand, Ireland risks leaving itself unnecessarily exposed to foreign intelligence and influence operations conducted not merely by hostile powers but potentially by friendly states as well.

Friendship between governments is no substitute for scrutiny.

Indeed, democracies generally discover that the activities which escape scrutiny are precisely the ones that later require it most.

The relevance of the American approach was underlined only recently when the US Department of Justice publicly reminded individuals that both FARA and 18 U.S.C. § 951 can impose disclosure or notification obligations on persons acting for foreign governments or foreign principals. 

The Department specifically referred to public demonstrations undertaken on behalf of a foreign power as an activity that may, depending on the circumstances, engage those requirements.⁶

And then there is the curious spectacle witnessed in Dublin this week.

The Ukrainian Embassy in Ireland announced publicly:

“Today in Dublin, we held a rally.”

The Embassy then urged Ireland and its international partners towards particular political and foreign-policy actions.

Whatever view one takes of Ukraine, Russia or the war itself, the principle deserves examination.

A foreign embassy organised a demonstration in the Irish capital and openly sought to influence Irish Government policy and Irish public opinion.

What did the Government of Micheál Martin do?

Apparently, nothing.

Yet Ukraine itself has repeatedly objected to Russian attempts to influence its domestic and political affairs.

On 12 March 2014, Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs formally described a Russian Foreign Ministry statement concerning Crimea as “direct and undisguised interference” in Ukraine’s internal affairs, arguing that it conflicted with fundamental principles of international law.⁷

The previous day, the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry had similarly condemned what it called Russia’s “direct intrusion” into Ukraine’s internal affairs.⁸

Principles are most persuasive when they survive the journey abroad.

If foreign political influence is objectionable when Moscow practises it in Ukraine, Ireland is entitled to ask where Kyiv believes legitimate diplomacy ends and political intervention begins when its own diplomatic mission is organising demonstrations in Dublin.

The question is not whether Ukraine is friend or foe.

The question is whether Ireland is sufficiently serious about its own sovereignty to apply transparent rules to everybody.

Because foreign influence does not cease to be foreign influence merely because we happen to like the country exercising it.

Ireland needs a modern foreign-agents law.

It needs transparency over foreign funding, foreign representation and foreign political activity.

And it needs a Government willing to recognise that countering hostile influence begins not with deciding which foreign governments we trust, but with ensuring that all of them play by clearly defined Irish rules.

The front door of a sovereign democracy should be open to diplomacy.

It does not follow that we should leave the keys under the mat.

text:
“I will share with you on the unlimited power of Child Protective Services. I served in the Georgia State Senate & after four years of viewing the ruthless & unsparing actions of Child Protective Services, also called CPS, which I will use tonight, I wrote a scathing report entitled ‘The Corrupt Business of Child Protective Services’ (Nov 16, 2007). The report cost me my Senate seat. However, there are causes worth losing over. And this is one.

This is not to say that there are not those children in wretched situations who need to be removed. There are and we all agree. 

But, tonight I’m talking about those children removed from their homes intentionally for profit. Children are seized unnecessarily from their families due to the federal aid created in 1974 entitled ‘The Adoption and Safe Families Act.’ It offers financial incentives to the states that increase adoption numbers. To receive the adoption incentives or bonuses, local CPS must have more children. They must have more merchandise to sell. Funding is available when a child is placed in a foster home with strangers or placed in a mental health facility and medicated, usually against the parents’ wishes. Parents are victimized by the system that makes a profit for holding children longer and bonuses for not returning children to their parents. This is abuse of power. It is lack of accountability. And it is a growing criminal political phenomenon spreading around the globe.

Often times, but not always, poor parents are targeted to lose their children because they do not have the wherewithal to hire an attorney or fight the system. Being poor and lacking proper housing does not mean your children should be removed. CPS has redefined ‘poor’ to mean psychologically inferior therefore it is in the best interest of the child to be removed. ‘Best interest’ has also been redefined at the child’s expense. 

It has been reported over and over that six times as many children die in foster care than in the general public. Once a child is legally kidnapped and placed in official safety, the child is far more likely to suffer abuse, including sexual, molestation, and/or rape.

Caseworkers and social workers are often guilty of fraud. They withhold and destroy evidence and they seek wrongly to terminate parental rights while being protected by state immunity.

There is a huge bureaucracy made up of judges, court-appointed attorneys, guardian ad litems, social workers, state employees, court investigators, therapists, psychologists, psychiatrists, foster parents, adoptive parents, and on and on, who are looking to the children in state care for their job security. Judges have control over private living arrangements and income of 48.3 million Americans. The @uscensusbureau reported in 2002 that $40 billion in transfer payments were made between households of custody parents and other parents. That money, $40 billion, is under the direction and control of family court judges in environments covered with confidentiality laws that protect the wrong people. 

Fathers are victims of this unjust system. Child support payments, even without having visits with their children, are choking the very life out of fathers. Three fathers of whom I am aware and have been in touch with committed suicide in the last 12 months because they lost the opportunity to even visit with their children. These are crimes against humanity for financial gain. Rights are removed from parents— human rights, civil rights, and even religious rights. 

I do not believe that a single child comes out whole after having been in this system. Many foster children make up the homeless population of today. An independent audit should be called on every state of all Child Protective Services departments.” ~Senator Nancy Schaefer

text:
Peter Thiel 十几年前讲过一个职业建议：

把「这件事写进简历好不好看」从人生决策里删掉。

当时 Thiel 在 UT Austin 宣传《Zero to One》，一个年轻工程师问他，应该怎么判断自己下一步该做什么。

Thiel 说，大多数人最大的问题，是把未来想得太模糊。

不知道自己最终要去哪里，于是每一步都开始为下一步服务。读研是为了拿一个更好的 offer，去咨询公司是为了下一份工作更好跳，进大厂是为了简历上多一行漂亮的公司名。

人生最后变成一棵不断分叉的职业树。

每个节点看起来都保留了更多选择，但你一直没有真正开始做自己想做的事情。

Thiel 给了一个很简单的判断方法，把未来拆成三个时间尺度。

短期：我在这里开心吗？每天有没有学到很多东西？

中期：这段经历写在简历上够不够漂亮？

长期：我做的事情到底重不重要，有没有意义？

他说，我们这个社会把太多精力花在了第二个问题上。

所以他的建议是多想短期，多想长期，忘掉中期。

这句话放到 2026 年，我觉得更重要。

因为 AI 正在让很多所谓的「中期资产」加速折旧。

一个过去能在简历上吃五年的 title，一套你花几年练出来的职业技能，一家曾经足够漂亮的公司名字，都可能因为模型、组织方式和行业周期的变化迅速贬值。

反过来，两个东西越来越难被替代。

你现在是不是处在一个学习密度足够高、自己真的愿意投入的环境里；

以及十年以后回头看，你现在做的事情究竟有没有积累出什么真正属于自己的东西。

当然，忘掉中期本身也是一句很 Thiel 的话。

对很多人来说，房租、签证、家庭责任、现金流都是真实存在的，你不可能完全不管简历和下一份工作。

但我很喜欢他想提醒的那件事：

职业规划最危险的状态，可能不是走错路，而是你每一步看起来都走得很对，最后却发现这条路从来不是你自己选的。

text:
Peter Thiel on how you should think about your future:

"What you end up doing when you think of the future as indefinite is you pick a job that you think will look good on your resume, because it will lead to a different job later on. There's even a credentialing version where you go to grad school, you get a consulting job, and you think of it as this branching tree diagram where you never really do something that you want to do.

You can think of the future on three horizons. Very short-term is: are you going to be happy, and will you be learning a lot? Medium-term is: how good is it on your resume? And very long-term is: are you working on something important or meaningful? We're in a skewed world where we overweight the medium-term and underweight some combination of the short-term and the long-term. I would recalibrate to focus on the short-term and the long-term, and forget about the medium-term."

text:
I truly thank God for life, health, and all the things He blesses me with daily, but I really think I was born in the wrong era.

I think that because of the year I was born and the conditions in which I was born, I may never experience some of the things that would truly make me happy. I may never be married. I may never witness some of the beautiful things that the Holy Bible and the Holy Quran speak of, besides Heaven and Paradise.

In this world, you are either too good or not good enough for people who constantly complain about the mediocrity in the world.

We live in a world where a good man is labeled lame, a square, boring, or a simp simply because he treats people right, is responsible, doesn’t physically abuse women, and doesn’t call women out of their names.

We will give someone money for coming home from prison after committing a crime they knew was wrong, but we won’t give our kids, nieces, nephews, or cousins money for college. We won’t give them the support they need to help jump-start their businesses or build something positive for themselves.

You can’t even be nice to people nowadays. You can’t simply speak to someone, hold a door open, give a compliment, or offer assistance without them thinking you want something in return.

You can’t have morals, values, standards, or refuse to settle nowadays because the moment you do, people ask, “Who hurt you?” Suddenly, you’re difficult. You’re asking for too much. You’re considered “too much” simply because you know what you want and what you’re unwilling to accept.

I really think I was born in the wrong era.

text:
St. Maurilius, Bishop of Angers by Fr. Francis Xavier Weninger, 1882
.
The native place of St. Maurilius was Milan, and his teacher was St. Martin, who had founded a monastery near that city, wherein he lived. After this holy man had been banished from Milan by the Arians, and had become Bishop of Tours, Maurilius went to him to be instructed in virtue and wisdom. When he had made sufficient progress, St. Martin ordained him priest, after which Maurilius repaired to Angers to preach the Gospel, as at that time, a great number of the inhabitants were pagans. While on this way thither, he saw the temple of an idol, standing near the river. Pitying the blindness of the people, he besought God to destroy this temple; when, behold, fire falls from heaven, the temple is overthrown, the idol burned to ashes! Maurilius, having had all the rubbish carried away, assisted by some pious Christians, built a church upon the same spot, together with a monastery in which he took up his abode with a number of devout men, whom he governed as Abbot. During this time he converted an almost countless number of pagans, as well in the city as out of it, by zealous preaching and the miracles he performed on the sick, the possessed and the blind.
.
Meanwhile the Bishop of Angers died, and St. Martin, who went thither to choose a successor, took Maurilius with him. The clergy and people were assembled, and the election was about to begin, when suddenly a white dove was seen which, after having fluttered through the church for some time, at length descended upon the shoulder of St. Maurilius. All looked upon this event as a sign that God had chosen this holy man as Bishop, and hence they unanimously declared that they desired no other. He was therefore consecrated bishop by St. Martin, to the inexpressible comfort of the people, although he himself shed many tears at being obliged to accept the dignity.
..
As Bishop, his virtues shone still more brightly; for he had more opportunities to practise them in the world than in the convent and his exalted station imparted to them an additional lustre. He fasted with great rigor, and on three days of the week he partook only of bread and salt. He never tasted wine, and during Lent, seldom left his residence; "for," said he, "Lent is a time of solitude, during which we ought to contemplate the passion and death of Christ." He was unwearied in instructing his flock and in converting the heathen.
.
One day, while he was standing before the Altar to perform the holy sacrifice, a woman requested him to administer to her sick son the holy sacrament of Confirmation. Maurilius, not thinking that the lad was in danger, continued Mass, but before he had finished it, the child was dead. The holy man was exceedingly grieved at this accident, and as if having committed great sin, he sentenced himself to a severe penance. He secretly left the city, and hastened over hill and dale, until having arrived at the sea, he went on board of a ship which was setting sail for England. During the voyage, the keys of the holy relics which he had taken with him, fell into the sea, and he solemnly declared that he would not return to his diocese, until he should again possess them, which, as he believed, would never happen.
.
At length he arrived in England, where, without making himself known, he took service with a nobleman as gardener. It was his intention to do penance for his sin by the hard labors of this occupation during winter and summer. The inhabitants of Angers were meanwhile greatly dismayed at the disappearance of their highly esteemed bishop, and sent several persons in search of him. Seven whole years had elapsed, when, by divine revelation they found him. Their good angel guided them in such a manner, that they found their holy bishop coming from his garden with a load of vegetables for his master. They immediately recognized him, and besought him, with tears in their eyes, to return to his see, and watch over the spiritual welfare of his flock. St. Maurilius, who thought that they had long since elected another bishop, was greatly disturbed on beholding them. He could not deny his identity, but endeavored to evade their wishes by making different pretexts, and finally declared that he could not return under any circumstances, as he had solemnly vowed that he would not see Angers again until, the keys were found which had fallen out of his hand into the sea.
.
"If this is the only obstacle to your return, we are able to remove it," said the delegates; "for on the voyage, we caught a fish, in whose stomach we found the keys." Showing them to him, they persuaded him to regard the finding of them as an unmistakable proof that God desired his return. Maurilius made no further resistance, but taking leave of the gentleman whom he had served, he returned to his see. It must also be stated that, shortly before the arrival of the delegates, while St. Maurilius was weeping bitterly over his sins, an angel had appeared to him and given him the assurance of their entire remission, which filled his heart with inexpressible joy. It would be difficult to describe the rejoicings of the inhabitants of the entire diocese on the return of their holy bishop. The Saint, however, first went to the place where the abovementioned lad had been buried seven years before. Having said his prayers with the utmost confidence in the power of God, he awakened the child from death, as is testified by St. Gregory of Tours and others. Those present had never so clearly comprehended how pious and holy a man God had bestowed upon them in their bishop, as at the moment of that startling event. Maurilius gave the lad the name of Renatus, which means "born again," and instructed him so carefully in all that pertains to a Christian life, that he afterwards became the successor of his holy teacher.
.
The remainder of his life the Saint passed in his habitual austerity, and in great zeal for the salvation of souls. When he had reached his ninetieth year, God revealed to him the hour of his departure. Preparing himself with the greatest solicitude, he ordered his grave to be dug, and after a short illness, gave up his soul to his Creator. At his funeral, besides other miracles which took place, two persons who had been blind from birth received their sight, and a man who had been paralyzed thirty-one years, regained the use of his limbs, on kissing the coffin in which the relics of the Saint reposed. Well worth considering are the words which the holy man spoke shortly before his death to those around him: "Ponder well," said he, "that your souls are bought at a great price: the precious blood of Jesus Christ."
.
PRACTICAL CONSIDERATIONS.
.
I. St. Maurilius hired himself as gardener to a nobleman, in order to atone for his sin. Sin must not only be repented of and confessed, but also expiated, as I have already told you. This expiation can be made by performing our work in the spirit of penance; by bearing patiently the cares and labors of our respective stations, by enduring heat and cold, sickness, poverty, persecution or wrong, and by offering all this to the Almighty as an atonement for our sins. This means should be employed by all those sinners who are either unable or unwilling to follow the example of so many holy penitents in the use of corporal austerities. As we cannot avoid labors, sufferings and hardships, let us labor and suffer patiently, and thus offer to God some atonement for our iniquities. The Council of Trent declares it a special proof of God's love, that we are permitted to atone, through the merits of Jesus Christ, for our sins, by bearing patiently the temporal evils that Providence lays upon us. Recognize and duly esteem this love, and act in accordance with my instructions.
.
II. Consider the last words of St. Maurilius. "Ponder well," said he, " that your souls are bought at a great price: the precious blood of Jesus Christ." This is a truth which ought to be impressed upon your heart. "For you are bought," says St. Paul, "with a great price." (I. Cor. vi.) St. Peter says: "Knowing that you were not redeemed by corruptible things, as gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb unspotted and undefiled. (1 Peter, i.) Christ has bought our souls with His blood. Hence, how priceless must they be in the sight of God, and how great should be our cure to secure their salvation! Our horror of sin ought indeed to be great, as, by our iniquities, we deprive Christ of the soul so dearly ransomed, and sell it to the spirit of hell, according to the words of Isaias: "Behold, you are sold for your iniquities." (Isaias,!) What was the price you received? The pleasure of a moment, as is said by St. Augustine. How dreadful a wickedness! Christ Jesus ransomed the souls of men with His precious blood, of which one drop is of more value than all the treasures of the world; and man sells his soul again to His most bitter enemy for a momentary pleasure, a short temporal advantage! How great a responsibility, how great a punishment must follow such astonishing wickedness! If you are guilty of such enormity, repent of it with bitter tears, and take your priceless soul forcibly from Satan by doing penance, and in future think more of the inestimable price with which it was bought by Christ; otherwise the blood of the Saviour will cry for vengeance against you on the Judgment-day. "Let us guard with great solicitude," writes Eusebius of Emesa, "what Christ bought with His precious blood. He who denies his soul, ransomed by the sufferings of Christ, is not guilty of less than the blood of the Saviour." St. Bernard says on the same subject: "If we neglect the soul, which Christ esteemed more precious than His own blood, we draw down upon ourselves not only eternal condemnation, but we shall also be most severely punished; as we, so to say, have trodden under our feet the blood of the Lamb."

text:
AIR Center’s analysis of President Ilham Aliyev’s speech at the 8th Congress of the New Azerbaijan Party.

➡️The speech moved on two tracks at once. Looking back, it traced a line from the party's founding congress and Heydar Aliyev's return to power in 1993 to the restoration of the country's territorial integrity in 2023. Looking forward, it named the tasks ahead - security, ideological resilience, an independent foreign policy, economic and financial stability, energy and transport, social policy and the Great Return to Garabakh (relocation of refugees back to their homes).
➡️Azerbaijan did not receive its territorial integrity as a gift. It restored it through a hard and costly fight, in three stages that the speech set out clearly: 1) the 44-day war, from 27 September to 10 November 2020, which ended in Armenia's defeat and capitulation; 2) three years of building the military and political ground for full sovereignty, from November 2020 to September 2023; 3) the anti-terror operation of 20 September 2023, which restored sovereignty over the whole territory and led to the withdrawal of all foreign armed forces.
➡️Having won, Azerbaijan now seeks peace. The peace agreement text, initialed with Armenia in Washington in August 2025, opened a real chance to advance sustainable peace in the years to come. But the lesson Baku draws from its own history is plain. Peace holds when the side that wants it is strong enough that no one is tempted to test it. As the speech put it, Azerbaijan must always be strong so that history does not repeat itself.
➡️The speech's security message starts from a sober reading of the world. Wars are being fought in Europe and the Middle East, great-power rivalry is sharpening, and the international rules that small states rely on are being openly ignored. The South Caucasus sits at the junction of these pressures. In such an environment, the risk of war cannot be dismissed simply because one conflict has ended.
➡️The President also set out a doctrine of deterrence in unusually direct terms. Azerbaijan, he said, does not leave a single blow against it unanswered, so that everyone stays in their place and does not interfere in its affairs. Its purpose is to make aggression too costly to contemplate.
➡️Two other pillars support this posture. The first is financial independence. The second is an independent, multi-vector foreign policy.
➡️Guarding the secular state: the most forward-looking part of the speech concerned ideological security. In a world of the internet, cyberattacks and artificial intelligence, the President warned, ideological sabotage knows no borders. A state can defend its frontiers with soldiers, but the minds of its citizens are defended by other means.
➡️Conclusion: the common thread is that sovereignty and territorial integrity, once restored, has to be defended every day and on every front. Azerbaijan has paid too high a price for its land to take peace for granted. It offers its neighbors a settlement based on mutual recognition of borders. But it will negotiate from strength, protect its secular identity from those who would import the conflicts of other regions, and rely, above all, on itself.

text:
WASHINGTON, NOT TEHRAN, IS NOW THE HOLDUP ON LOCKHEED $LMT'S NEXT MISSILE ORDERS:

Lockheed Martin (LMT) at $505.41, -$0.09 / -0.02% on Friday.

That is -$15.54 / -2.98% from the quoted post's $520.95. Friday was its seventh lower close in a row and its lowest since June 29. It also sits below the $514.36 close of July 22. The next morning Lockheed reported a record $230.4B backlog - work signed but not yet delivered. The gains from that report, and from the Patriot interceptor contract signed a week later, are gone.

The verdict: the peace offer the quoted post weighed was dead within four days, and the stock kept sliding. The brake on Lockheed's next orders that did show up came from Congress. The temporary budget that took over on October 1 does not pay for the bigger Patriot orders the Pentagon has already negotiated. The demand is intact. The money for its next step is on hold until at least December 11.

The quoted post's explanation failed its own test. On Saturday, September 26, President Trump said Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz "would not be acceptable." The Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November 3 midterm elections. A stock knocked down by peace talk should have bounced. Lockheed has lost more since the rejection than it did on the day the offer arrived:

- September 22, the day of the offer: -$13.06 / -2.44%.
- Since September 25, the last close before the rejection: -$14.15 / -2.72%.

Nobody publishes why a stock falls, but this one moved with its industry, not on news of its own:

- iShares US Aerospace and Defense ETF (ITA) at $207.79, -$0.25 / -0.12% on Friday.
- SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) at $769.64, +$5.65 / +0.74% on Friday.

Since the September 25 close, the defense fund is down 2.8%, about what Lockheed lost. The S&P 500 fund is down 0.2%.

What took hold across that whole industry on October 1 was a budget, not a ceasefire. On September 2, President Trump signed a stopgap - a temporary budget that keeps last year's spending going - that funds the government through Friday, December 11. It started when the federal fiscal year began. It keeps weapons programs at last year's funding and holds production at last year's rate. The White House had asked for an exception letting the Pentagon fund five missile programs at the quantities it negotiated, Lockheed's Patriot interceptor among them. It warned the Pentagon "may incur cancellation liabilities on multi-year procurement contracts if it does not order the negotiated production quantities." Congress left the exception out.

That lands where the quoted post said Lockheed was growing fastest. On July 29 the Pentagon signed a contract for PAC-3 interceptors, the missiles Patriot batteries fire, worth up to $58.62B over seven years. It is built to triple production capacity by the end of 2030, and its final terms are still being negotiated. Tripling capacity only pays if each year's order is bigger than the last. Until December 11, the stopgap does not pay for a bigger one.

The quoted post feared a ceasefire would slow the refills that built Lockheed's $87.9B missile backlog. The ceasefire never came. The refill money has not come yet either. Smaller orders kept arriving right up to the freeze: on September 29 the Pentagon announced more than $1B of Lockheed work, $724M of it for Aegis combat systems on two Japanese warships.

The second change is what safe money pays. The 10-year Treasury yield, the rate the US government pays to borrow for a decade, went from 4.96% on September 22 to 5.28% on Friday, by the Treasury's daily count.

That eats into Lockheed's discount. At $505.41 the stock costs 16.7 times the middle of the $29.95-$30.65 a share Lockheed expects to earn this year. Turned around, each $100 of stock buys about $6.00 of this year's expected profit, up from $5.82 at the quoted post's price. A $100 Treasury now pays $5.28 a year, up from $4.96. The stock got cheaper, and the bond got better faster. Lockheed's lead over the bond narrowed from about 0.86 of a percentage point to 0.72.

Lockheed is still on the Quality-Value Len5, which hunts a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought under its worth. The first half has not moved: nobody stands up a second Patriot or F-35 line. It now ranks 58th of the Len5's 72 names, down from 20th of 61 when the quoted post ran. On the math above, the half under pressure is the discount, not the business. What would knock Lockheed off the Quality-Value Len5: an October 22 cut to that $29.95-$30.65 range, because the discount is measured against the company's own number.

One correction to the quoted post: Lockheed reports on Thursday, October 22, before the open, with a call at 8:30am ET. The quoted post printed a tentative Tuesday, October 20; Lockheed confirmed the 22nd on October 1. Analysts still expect $7.41 a share, against $6.95 a year earlier.

That report covers the quarter that ended September 27, before the stopgap took hold, so its orders figure looks backward. The number that decides this verdict looks forward: what Lockheed says about next year's Patriot quantities while the money waits. Then comes December 11, when Congress passes a full-year defense budget, extends the stopgap, or lets funding lapse. The key risk is a second stopgap. Every month without a full-year budget is another month the bigger orders wait.

Every week of the war adds to the case for more Patriot interceptors. Congress, which writes the checks, has not yet agreed to pay for them.

Not investment advice.

text:
It sounds like you were referring to filling up the gas tank rather than tag registration, but most of the replies are about tags.

Around 2000, Priceline offered the ability to bid for low gas prices the way they do hotel fares. It was highly successful. That’s when we still had the federal rule that didn’t allow state taxes on online purchases. The savings people enjoyed was not paying the state sales tax on tax as well as negotiated fleet pricing via the Priceline app. After a couple years, states got the loophole closed. I miss it.

As for tags, I have a friend in Clark County with a 2006 Tundra. He drove on expired tags for three years rather than pay $160. A county sheriff pulled him over and was letting him off with a warning when a state cop joined and wrote him a ticket. The sheriff stayed until the state cop left, then reminded my friend that Washington allows deferring one moving and one non-moving violation every seven years for a $150 fee. He filed for the deferral; it was approved automatically and gave him two years to pay. His wife found out and made him renew his tags. He paid $310 for four years of tags, $77.50 per year. Sometimes one has to play the game as written.

text:
HKUST Develops Self-Sustaining Seawater-to-Hydrogen System

A research team from HKUST, in collaboration with Arizona State University (ASU) and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU), has developed a sustainable integrated seawater-to-hydrogen system that can produce hydrogen directly from seawater while converting waste heat from electrolysis into a resource for producing the purified water required for hydrogen production. By integrating hydrogen production, water generation, and thermal management into a single system, the technology could help reduce the reliance of green hydrogen production on freshwater resources and offer a new approach for sustainable hydrogen development in water-scarce regions.

The study was led by Prof. SHANG Chii, Professor of the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at HKUST, and Dr. Gabriela Scheibel CASSOL, a postdoctoral fellow in the same department and an HKUST PhD graduate in Environmental Engineering. The research team also included Prof. Paul WESTERHOFF of Arizona State University and corresponding author Dr. SONG Yinghao, a postdoctoral fellow at PolyU and HKUST PhD graduate in Civil Engineering. The research was published in Nature Communications, titled “Thermally symbiotic integration of osmotic membrane distillation and electrolysis for direct seawater hydrogen production.”

Find more about the Self-Sustaining Seawater-to-Hydrogen System in the comments.

text:
A Man Always Knows From the Start… 

Apparently, when Tayfun had returned from Istanbul, he had also brought back a ring with him that used to belong to his mother. That is what he handed to me when he proposed to me in Starbucks in November that year, a few months after we met. Don’t get me wrong, it was actually a very beautiful Starbucks and the ambiance was perfect.

Tayfun told me that he had had this on his mind from the get-go. It turns out he knew in his heart the moment he met me that I was his destiny and that he would marry me. He always tells me I am his until infinity.
Some changes were necessary for our new life together. He gave up his apartment and moved in to my place in Virginia for a few months until we got our own place.

We had a very private wedding ritual prior to our actual marriage. There were only three people in attendance: Myself, Tayfun and God. We unified ourselves by making a promise between the three of us.

For our formal marriage, we had a very small ceremony. It was actually just the two of us and it was beautiful.

Personally, I still can’t believe I’m married. It feels like a dream, so surreal. Life has put me through so much trauma, so much sadness that I find it really hard to believe that that very same life has now given me so much joy. I always offer my gratitude to God.

A week after we got married my cat, Efecan, became extremely unwell. We had to take him to the vet because his kidneys were failing. It was crushing to see him like that. I was devastated as he couldn’t make it and passed away. Only people who have that special bond with their pets will understand how crippling this was.

During that phase, Tayfun was my rock and the support he gave me was priceless.

He carried me right through it.
