text:
The State v The Government: A sobbering lecture by an old man. Please read🙏

A few days ago, while hosting Raymond Mujuni in his podcast,  Yusuf Sserunkuma made a teaser announcement that Raymond is about to join the "government"(in quotes for a purpose). Raymond affirmed the teaser. Call it testing waters

The reaction from the online community was immidiate. Many marked him as a "target" since he has joined the "enemy". Some few gave him a pat on the back and offered best wishes.

I am not here to judge either side. Neither to judge Raymond. I am just offering a sobbering lesson that I received from an old man (he was 93 years then-5 years ago). He sat me down and took me through his memory lane. Having worked in the colonial administration,  Obote 1, Amin, Yusuf Lule and Binaisa and the start of Obote 2 before he hanged his uniform. He opened my mind a lot. He recounted, in vivid details, the works that he and countless others did to ensure the state structure remains amidst the challenges of the times.

He said, in every nation, there are two abstract entities; a state and a government. That a nation can survive (not prosper, but survive) without a government but a government cannot exist without a state. I had heard this in theory but had never given it deep, philosophical thoughts.

He gave an example of the UK where the Crown is the state and 10 Downing Street is the government. He told me the government can collapse (and is often disolved) but the state always remains to construct the government.

I know someone is about to interject and say that's an inappropriate comparison to a country like Uganda since that's a monarchical system of one thousand years.

I would respond to that person that the construct of every modern state is premised on the UK governance architecture. Some have made modifications but the central column still remain more UKish. 

The most vivid example we have, on state v government, in modern history is Somalia. Upto 1991, Somalia had a centralised government. When Mohamed Said Barre was overthrown, the country disintegrated into clan based regional power centres. It has taken AMISOM donkey years to try to rearrange the spokes of the government wheel. It is doing this by trying to reconstruct the state. A toll order,  but we hope they succeed.

Why have I laboured to bring my lecture and statecraft parallels to Raymond's impending joining of "government"?

Raymond himself admitted that he is joining the civil service side of government. For those who know, civil service bureaucracy is the spinal cord of the state. Not government. President Museveni spent his formative years of his government fighting with this bureaucracy because he felt it was not aligned to his ideologies (not sure what he meant but you can dig up his public spat with the civil service)

In that bureaucracy,  we need honest, hardworking, patriotic and intelligent people like Raymond and others. They do things that holds the structure of the state even when the government disintegrates as we have seen in the past. 

The old man told me the same. That even when Amin's government ravaged the economy and the general governance space, state apparatus such as the prison,  police, army, border controls, revenue collection, budget systems, school etc remained limping but operational. Some even thrived. If all these had collapsed, president Museveni would have probably failed in everything because he wouldnt know where tonstart from. He had a solid, though cracked base to start from.

You may argue that by him joining "government " he and others (who were/are either critical or in stark opposition to president Museveni's leadership), he is strengthening the "dictatorship" to as to trample you/us more. You could have a valid argument. However, people who understands statecraft, will know the Raymonds will (in sha Allah) mend and build a stronger foundation for the state of Uganda that other government will build on in future. 1/2

text:
Schneider Electric on October 5, 2026 said it will buy U.S. industrial software company PTC in an all-cash deal at $205 a share, valuing PTC's equity at about $22.6 billion and implying a $23.7 billion enterprise value.

The offer is a 42.3% premium to PTC's last close and a 46.1% premium to its prior 30-day volume-weighted average. Closing is targeted for the third quarter of 2027, subject to PTC shareholder approval and regulators. Schneider expects about €250 million of annual run-rate cost synergies by year three and roughly €800 million of revenue synergies, and plans to fund the roughly €22 billion cash outlay with about €5 to €6 billion of new equity and €16 to €17 billion of new debt.

CEO Olivier Blum cast the deal as building an industrial software and AI franchise that bridges product design with energy and process data, alongside Schneider's earlier agreement to buy Cognite. PTC CEO Neil Barua said the all-cash sale maximises shareholder value. Sunday media reports that Schneider was "nearing" a deal are superseded by Monday's definitive agreement.

Why it matters: one of Europe's biggest industrial tech groups is paying a software multiple to own the CAD and product-lifecycle layer that feeds industrial AI. Sources: Schneider Electric / PTC, 5 Oct 2026; Reuters, 5 Oct 2026.

🚨 THE $1B CONTRACT ERROR: EARLY NVIDIA ADVISOR LOSES FORTUNE OVER 1993 PAPERWORK! 💻💸

An early Nvidia advisor revealed how a 30-year-old vesting mistake cost him $1.05 Billion in NVDA stock! 👇

🔹 The 1993 Grant: Eric Gullichsen was offered 25,000 options in 1993. A signed contract specified 1-year vesting, but Nvidia applied a 4-year clock, shorting him 9,375 options.

🔹 $468 to $1.05B: After 480x stock splits, those missing options equal 4.5M shares worth $1.05B today!

text:
I drew a clear, unambiguous boundary, and you crossed it without hesitation in the heat of the moment. You didn't do it by accident; you did it because whatever basic respect you had for me had completely evaporated. You believed you could violate my boundaries, treat me with contempt, and that there would still be no consequences.

And now, when you feel the doors finally locking, you send this calculated, manipulative message. You claim you "respect my decision" while simultaneously denying the reality of your actions, writing off your documented deceit as just "ugly things" I said, and condescendingly suggesting I just needed "time to calm down." You dangle nostalgia about marriage and family, bring up taking care of you after your surgery to weaponize my guilt, and offer vague, empty promises to "work on your fears and confidence." It is an insult to my intelligence. You don't take accountability for a single lie, for using me as a financial buffer, or for disrespecting me—you are just scrambling to see if soft words can stop the boxes from leaving.

The truth is, as much as my heart wanted to protect you from pain, I realize now that I haven't been helping you at all. For months, I cushioned every single fall. I funded your life, absorbed your disrespect, solved your crises, and stood between you and the natural laws of cause and effect. By trying to spare you the suffering of your own mistakes, I only prolonged your immaturity and enabled your stagnation.

You are an adult who has acted like a reckless child, and real growth will never happen for you inside the luxury shelter I provided. Growth only comes from bearing the cold, heavy weight of your own actions. Walking away and letting you face the consequences of the wreckage you created is not cruelty—it is the only real teacher left for you.

The moment you felt comfortable, the moment you extracted what you thought you needed, the mask slipped entirely. Suddenly, the devotion evaporated. Suddenly, you don't believe in me or this relationship anymore. You convinced yourself of whatever lie was convenient at the time to justify taking from me, and now that you've drained what you could, you treat me with utter disrespect and act like none of it ever mattered.

When you spoke about the life and healing you wanted, I didn't just listen—I executed. My entire intention was to create a sheltered, safe environment where you never had to feel inadequate or struggle again. I knew the visceral pain you carried from your past, how much being fat and treated poorly had broken your self-worth, and how deeply having a new body meant finally feeling worthy and secure in your own skin. I paid for that surgery and nursed you through recovery not just as an expense, but as an act of profound care to heal that wound. Alongside that, I paid for your education, financed the beginnings of your nail salon business, and equipped you with the tools for interior design by buying a high tech iPad because I genuinely believed in investing in the woman I thought was my future wife.

But the more I gave to heal and build you, the more distorted your reality became. What began as voluntary, deeply empathetic provision quickly morphed into your baseline expectation. You stopped showing genuine gratitude and started treating massive personal and financial sacrifices like standard maintenance. You took the safety, the upgraded body, and the life I bankrolled, normalized it, and turned it into cold entitlement. You didn't fall in love with me or appreciate the grace you received; you became entitled to the emotional repair, the capital, and the lifestyle I made possible.

text:
U.S. "defense" spending is set to reach approximately $961 billion in fiscal year 2026, while the national debt surpasses the $39 trillion to $40 trillion range during the same period. Critics characterize this combination—a debt-laden nation maintaining the world's largest military budget—as a fiscal manifestation of "imperial overstretch." A deeper structural issue lies in the fact that defense spending has created a self-perpetuating cycle of interests; Congress, the Pentagon, contractors, and lobbying groups form a machine that was "never designed to stop."

A Comparison of Figures
Debt vs. Defense. CBO projections from February 2026 indicate that federal debt will reach 101% of GDP in 2026 and rise to 120% by 2036, surpassing the historic peak of 106% set in 1946. Meanwhile, the Department of Defense's base budget request for 2026 stands at $961 billion—one of the largest requests in the past 50 years when adjusted for inflation. The Congressional Budget Office notes that 2025 tax legislation increased spending on defense and homeland security, while net interest costs reached $1.0 trillion in 2026, exceeding spending in numerous budget categories other than defense.

The Cost of Overseas Bases. The United States maintains over 750 military bases in more than 80 countries, housing approximately 200,000 troops stationed abroad. Although the maintenance costs for these bases are not itemized separately, they form the physical foundation for "global power projection" and represent fixed expenditures that cannot be easily cut from the budget.

The Cycle of Interests: Who Keeps the Machine Running
CBO analysis clearly indicates that the 2025 reconciliation act "increased spending on defense and homeland security," thereby driving up deficit projections. Yet, this is not merely a story of the government deciding to spend more money. It is a structure defined by the intertwining interests of multiple parties:

Contractor Contributions. A May 2026 report by *Military Times* revealed that the defense sector—comprising traditional giants like Lockheed Martin, RTX, and Northrop Grumman, as well as emerging defense-tech firms like Anduril—donated nearly $5 million to members of Congress through political action committees (PACs) and individual contributions. These funds flowed to decision-makers capable of influencing defense procurement legislation, including Ken Calvert, Chair of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee (who received approximately $200,000), and Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee (who received nearly $130,000).

The "Revolving Door." A 2026 report by the *Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists* documented 31 former members of Congress and senior staffers who joined the military-industrial complex as lobbyists or contractors after leaving Capitol Hill. Of these 31 individuals, 21 had served on the House or Senate Armed Services Committees—the very bodies that set Pentagon policy by passing the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Report author John Mecklin offered a blunt conclusion: "This is the most straightforward explanation we have ever published regarding why the defense budget always goes up."

A New Entry Point from Silicon Valley. A new wave of defense-tech companies is replicating this model. Palmer Luckey’s Anduril is valued at $61 billion; Luckey himself is one of the most significant Republican "bundlers" on the West Coast, hosting and co-hosting fundraisers for figures such as Trump, Ken Calvert, Rick Scott, and Ted Cruz. An August 2026 event required a $50,000 donation per guest, with the goal of "holding the Senate."

"Defending to Justify Spending"
The observation shared in your post—that "an empire does not spend money to defend itself, but rather defends itself to justify spending money"—finds a concrete parallel in the logic of budget structures.

In its analysis of the 2025 reconciliation bill, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) found that the Department of Defense primarily allocated reconciliation funds toward procurement, while noting that "procurement funding in the base budget was lower than expected." The CBO’s assessment is that "this pattern suggests that supplemental funds are substituting for—rather than merely supplementing—base budget resources." To put it more plainly: when Congress approves large, one-off allocations, the Pentagon does not view them as "extra" money but rather as a substitute for regular budget funding. This implies that the growth in spending is not a response to threats, but an adaptation to the sources of funding.

An Unstoppable Machine
The CBO’s long-term projections describe the debt trajectory as "unsustainable." But what does "unsustainable" mean in political practice? It means that the system will eventually be forced to change, or it will simply keep running until that change occurs. The observation in the post you shared—that the system was "never designed to stop"—holds up structurally: 31 former lawmakers and staffers joining the military-industrial complex over a decade, 31 congressional districts reliant on defense manufacturing jobs, and a network built on campaign donations, lobbying, and the "revolving door"—none of these are the products of "threat assessments." They are the products of the spending itself.

The Sovereign Oath

The strain is an oath treated as a contract with an outside authority, so the zero-point never gets spoken from the cell.

Where the strain comes from

The source stands at the zero-point and looks out. The declaration is not parchment and not a plea. It is a sovereign oath from cellular remembrance, in the tone of the high-priest frequency, meant to move through lattice, water, and the helix. Strain begins when that vow is outsourced: borrowed voltage, a middle owner of the blueprint, a performance of humility instead of the still axis. Five pillars are the seal. Candor transmits without packaging. Decorum holds the axis so every movement does not throw an acoustic wake. Free will is the mandorla, an open gate, not a push. Compassion makes no rank between flesh, stone, water, and vacuum. Service puts humanity first and anchors the 3-6-9 flux so the original design can be remembered. Without the seal, the note is sounded toward someone else.

When it locks

- Candor is filtered by commercial packaging or an artificial authority
- Decorum is performed, so the axis spins with the vortex
- Free will is steered, forced, or given a timeline
- Compassion is ranked, and matter is treated as dead
- Service waits for permission, and the chest never takes the vow

What the body is doing

The helix is trying to carry the oath in cell division, not in a document. The spine is the unmoving axis. The chest is the chalice. Overlapping circles make the vesica. The mandorla is the gateway offered, not imposed. The cross inside that lens is the still anchor: horizontal field, vertical remembrance. Water, stone, and the vacuum are the same living memory. text:
Inside a concrete prison cell in Nuremberg, Hermann Göring stripped away the grand illusions of warfare. Speaking quietly to an American army psychologist, the former Reichsmarschall offered no apologies and no remorse for the catastrophic destruction of Europe. Stripped of his jewel-encrusted medals, tailored uniforms, and paracodeine addiction, the second-most powerful man in the Third Reich was awaiting his sentence before the International Military Tribunal. Observers expected fanatical dogma or legal evasions. Instead, in an intimate exchange with intelligence officer Gustave Gilbert, Göring delivered a cold, clinical analysis of political power. With brutal nonchalance, the architect of Nazi rearmament explained that ordinary citizens never desire war, yet any government on earth—dictatorship or democracy alike—can effortlessly herd its population onto the battlefield.

The man on the iron cot was a shadow of his former public persona, yet mentally formidable. When captured in Austria in May 1945, Göring was bloated and carrying thousands of narcotic pills. Confined behind the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, prison warden Colonel Burton C. Andrus enforced a strict regimen. Deprived of drugs and placed on standard rations, Göring shed eighty pounds, regaining an oratorical sharpness that frequently outmaneuvered chief American prosecutor Robert H. Jackson. Captain Gustave Gilbert, a German-speaking psychologist holding a doctorate from Columbia University, enjoyed daily access to the defendants' cells to document their psychological profiles. Testing placed Göring’s intelligence quotient at 138, among the highest in the prison. During their quiet evening visits, Gilbert probed the inner mechanics of the regime, finding a prisoner who spoke with unsettling candor.

The decisive exchange occurred on April 18, 1946, during a recess in the proceedings. Gilbert stopped by cell number five to discuss the trial's evidence regarding the outbreak of the war, remarking that ordinary people were unlikely to feel grateful toward leaders who brought them ruins. Göring shrugged in contempt. "Why, of course, the people don't want war," Göring replied. "Why would some poor slob on a farm want to risk his life in a war when the best that he can get out of it is to come back to his farm in one piece?" It was a universal truth across all borders: common people never wanted conflict, whether in Russia, Britain, America, or Germany. But that reluctance was politically irrelevant. In the end, Göring explained, leaders determined national policy, and it was "always a simple matter to drag the people along."

Gilbert pushed back, seeking to defend the moral legitimacy of representative government. In a democracy, the psychologist argued, citizens possessed a constitutional voice through their elected representatives, and in the United States, only Congress held the authority to declare war. Göring brushed the objection aside as naive civics. "Oh, that is all well and good," he answered, "but, voice or no voice, the people can always be brought to the bidding of the leaders. That is easy." The mechanism required neither genius nor complicated persuasion: "All you have to do is tell them they are being attacked and denounce the pacifists for lack of patriotism and exposing the country to danger." He paused to emphasize the universal durability of the technique: "It works the same way in any country."

Göring was not sharing an abstract theory; he was describing the operational blueprint he had lived. In August 1939, to justify invading Poland to a populace that dreaded another war, the regime staged the Gleiwitz incident, faking a border attack by SS men disguised in Polish uniforms. text:
📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
        October 5, 1876

Six great powers order a sultan to stop a war. He says yes so cleverly that his "yes" is really a plan to finish his enemy off. It takes a 48-hour ultimatum, with one day to spare, to save a country from the map.

By the autumn of 1876, Serbia was losing badly. It had gone to war against the Ottoman Empire in support of the Balkan Christian revolts, and its army was being driven back toward Belgrade. On October 5, 1876, the great powers of the European Concert, threatening to break off diplomatic relations, demanded that the Porte grant Serbia an immediate armistice, to be followed by a conference to settle peace in the East. Six powers spoke with one voice: Russia, Britain, France, Austria-Hungary, Germany and Italy.

The Ottoman government answered the "concert of Europe" with a shrewd maneuver. On October 10 the Porte agreed to an armistice, and generously offered to make it last a full six months. The gesture looked peace-loving. In reality it was the opposite. A six-month truce would push any actual peace far into the future, giving Turkey time to rest and refit its army and then reopen the war in the spring, at a season of its choosing, against an exhausted Serbia.

Austria-Hungary was content to see it, and so was Britain; France did not object either. As one account put it, the cabinets wanted nothing better than to let the armistice talks drag on and give the Turks time to wear the Serbs down.

Russia refused to play along. On October 14 it rejected the Turkish offer and advised Serbia to turn down so long a truce. But Serbia's position was growing desperate, Prince Milan was pleading for help, and Russian prestige as the protector of the Balkan Slavs was on the line.

On October 15, at Livadia in the Crimea, a special council met under the Tsar. Chancellor Gorchakov, the war minister Milyutin, the finance minister Reutern and the ambassador to Turkey, Ignatiev, were there. The peace party argued for restraint. The council decided to press for a conference at Constantinople on the future of the Christian provinces, and to mobilize the army only if the conference failed. Mobilization would not yet mean war. It would be a lever to make Turkey yield. But if war proved unavoidable, Russia would start it at once, that winter, after arranging passage for its troops through Romania and at least the neutrality of Austria-Hungary.

Then, on October 31, 1876, Ignatiev handed the Porte an ultimatum: grant Serbia an immediate armistice of six weeks to two months, with an answer required within 48 hours, or Russia would break off diplomatic relations. The frightened Porte accepted at once. It gave up its plan to stretch the war to the spring, and with it the hope of crushing Serbia before any truce took hold.

How close it had been is clear from what the Serbs themselves admitted afterward. Their army had just been broken in the field, and the road to Belgrade lay open. Had the ultimatum come a single day later, the Turks would have taken Belgrade and ruined Serbia for good.

The conference Russia wanted met at Constantinople that December and failed, as the Ottomans, quietly encouraged by Britain, refused real reform. Within months Russia stopped relying on ultimatums and acted on the other half of the Livadia plan. In April 1877 it declared war on Turkey, opening the great Russo-Turkish War that would redraw the map of the Balkans.

text:
Chicago has promised $50.6 billion in pensions. It has $14.2 billion saved.

If I got hired to fix it, here's what I'd do differently from what City Hall has done for decades. Full math in the video.

That's 28 cents for every dollar promised and a $36.4 billion hole. 80 cents of every city property tax dollar now goes to pensions, up from 41 cents in 2014.

At a 7% assumed return, the hole costs about $2.5 billion a year just to stand still. Pay about $2.9 billion and it's gone in roughly 30 years. That's roughly $400 million a year between treading water and actually winning. Last year the city came up about half a billion short.

1. Pay what the funds need, not what's convenient.
For decades, state law set the city's payment as a fixed multiple of what workers paid in, not what the funds needed, and the funded ratio fell by more than two thirds after 2000. I'd pay the full actuarial bill every single year.

2. Set a deadline that doesn't move.
Current law targets 90% funded by 2055 and 2058, with most of the payments pushed to the back end. Police and fire were supposed to hit 90% by 2040 before that got pushed back. I'd target 100% on a fixed 30 year schedule. No extensions.

3. Make the extra payments mandatory.
Since 2023 the city has paid about $689 million more than the law requires. Right direction, but it's optional. This year a $260 million extra payment the City Council required got split in two before the city committed to the second half. I'd write it into law.

4. Don't touch what people already earned.
Emanuel's 2014 law trimming benefit increases for municipal workers and laborers was struck down by the Illinois Supreme Court in 2016. I'd offer voluntary buyouts instead: a smaller lump sum now for a bigger benefit later. Members choose, and it's paid with cash, not new debt.

5. Send every windfall to the hole.
Chicago has a habit of using one time money, like the 2008 parking meter lease, to plug the operating budget. Windfalls like TIF surplus would go straight to pensions.

6. Stop digging, including in Springfield.
The 2025 police and fire benefit bill passed almost unanimously, even though the city's CFO warned it could add $11 billion to the unfunded liability. No new benefits without the money attached.

Two more: pool the four funds' investments into one to cut fees, and grow the base so the same bill gets split more ways.

What doesn't change is the revenue fight. Emanuel's record 2015 property tax hike went mostly to police and fire pensions, and casino tax money is already earmarked for the same funds. New revenue or a constitutional amendment on future benefit growth is a call for voters. This plan doesn't make that choice go away. It makes sure whatever gets raised actually shrinks the hole.

The math only rules out one option: waiting.

The city’s recapture on October 3 is a major setback for the Tigrayan movement. It does not mean the war is over.

The balance of power is also shifting within Tigray. The Tigray Peace Force, which includes former Tigrayan fighters now allied with Addis Ababa, took part in the advance into Mekelle. On October 4, Abraham Belay, a former head of the interim administration, announced preparations for a new regional administration and elections “in a few months.” The timeline, the administration’s makeup, and public acceptance remain uncertain.

For civilians, the partial restoration of phone and internet service offers some initial relief. But looting was reported during the TPLF’s withdrawal, most businesses remained closed on Sunday, and the resumption of flights to Mekelle has not been confirmed. The priority now is to restore security, essential services, and humanitarian access.

The crisis also extends beyond Tigray diplomatically. On October 4, the leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia met in El Alamein. Their declaration calls for peaceful solutions while asserting that governance of the Red Sea belongs to its coastal states. The statement comes as Addis Ababa seeks access to the sea and accuses some of these neighbors of supporting its opponents. Those countries deny the allegations.

⚠️ It would be premature to declare either an end to the fighting or Eritrea’s entry into the war: neither has been established. The 2022 Pretoria agreement remains central to the question: How can another military victory in Mekelle be prevented from turning into a prolonged war across the rest of Tigray?

Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, the Ethiopian News Agency (ENA), and the official El Alamein declaration, October 4–5.

🇮🇷|The Strait of Hormuz is in Iran's hands: "US, you’ve gotten used to our rules...you’d better keep getting used to them."

~ Alaeddin Boroujerdi, a member of the Iranian Parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, issued this blunt declaration to the US from Tehran.

📢 What Boroujerdi said

Alaeddin Boroujerdi, a member of the Iranian Parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, made a statement to reporters regarding the latest situation between Iran and the US while attending the memorial service for Foreign Minister Araghchi's sister.

His core message was summed up in a single sentence:

"The Islamic Republic of Iran maintains firm and solid control over the Strait of Hormuz, and this situation will continue. This is Iran's policy, and it will not change."

Regarding Trump's threats, Boroujerdi said: "Trump has consistently used threatening language toward Iran; this is nothing new. We are already accustomed to Trump's rhetoric and the unconventional statements made by US presidents."

Regarding US military options, Boroujerdi offered a precise assessment: "In principle, the US will not enter a tense military or combat scenario prior to the congressional elections. However, should they choose to do so, the armed forces and the people of the Islamic Republic of Iran are fully prepared."

His conclusion: "By every metric, we are the winners in the context of the Strait of Hormuz, and this policy will remain steadfast."

🎯 Why Boroujerdi's statement reflects reality

Consider the reality of the Strait of Hormuz:

◽ The Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) has placed 81 vessels on a "non-compliance list," imposing fines, detentions, or confiscations on offending ships.
◽ The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has repeatedly launched anti-ship cruise missiles from the southern coastal city of Sirik, targeting vessels navigating unauthorized shipping lanes.
◽ Three tankers owned or chartered by the UAE the *Al RUWAIS, *SINBAD, and *MERSIN PROSPERITY have been targeted due to repeated violations.  
◽A supertanker capable of carrying 2.5 million barrels of oil was struck and set ablaze 8 kilometers off the coast of Oman.
◽ Oil tankers traversing the Strait of Hormuz are shutting off their AIS signals en masse, as the strait has effectively become a "black box."

Who controls Hormuz?

Not the United States. The U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain has been destroyed by Iran. U.S. forces will not be returning anytime soon.

It is Iran through its people, its soldiers, and its missiles.

🔥 Boroujerdi says "We won" and this is no mere rhetoric.

The U.S. has been fighting for six months. Iranian missiles are still flying. Iranian oil is still being sold. Iranian enriched uranium is still spinning in centrifuges.

Cumulative U.S. casualties in the conflict with Iran have reached 838: 18 dead and 820 wounded.

The Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain was destroyed. The Combined Air Operations Center at Al Udeid Air Base took a direct hit. An E-3 early-warning aircraft was destroyed. Nearly 60 U.S. aircraft were destroyed or damaged. Equipment losses total $3.7 billion.

Yet Iran, a nation sanctioned for over forty years, bombarded for six months, and having suffered the assassination of its Supreme Leader is still launching missiles.

That is the definition of "winning."

🛡️ "The U.S. won't escalate to a state of military tension before the election."

Boroujerdi’s assessment reveals a fact deliberately ignored by Western media:

Trump has linked the timeline for ending the war to the midterm elections. He stated himself: "I think the war will end immediately after the election."

But the battlefield does not shift to accommodate election schedules. Iran will not "collapse" because of the U.S. midterm elections just as it did not collapse during the preceding six months.

If the U.S. escalates before the election, it will face a fully prepared Iran. If it escalates after the election, it will face an even more united and determined Iran.

In either scenario, the U.S. cannot win.
